item.content:encoded:
Dezeen Showroom: Villeroy & Boch has published several of its new bathroom products on Dezeen Showroom, highlighting creative and sophisticated tapware, basins and vanity units.

Among the products is the Vea tapware, a lever-less design by German industrial designer Christian Haas based on his search for what he describes as "sensual reduction".

Haas looked to the design language of classic perfume bottles for the faceted design, which is available in black or white ceramic.

The form is intended to be sculptural yet calm and capable of blending into different bathroom settings, with one central button in place of a lever reducing visual noise.

A bold basin design comes from Roberto Palomba for Villeroy & Boch subsidiary Ideal Standard, who together have created Tipo-Z, a statuesque pedestal basin with a tapered, aerodynamic-looking silhouette.

Available in black or white, the basin is made of Ideal Standard's durable fireclay material, which allows for the realisation of its precisely defined edges.

Other new products from Villeroy & Boch use a new material developed with German design studio KaschKasch using 100 per cent recycled ceramic that is 3D printed.

Titled Antao 3D, the material is made entirely from the company's own production waste and carries subtle variations created in the process of layered printing.

The material builds on KaschKasch and Villeroy & Boch's Antao collection, which is focused on bringing elements from nature into the bathroom and also celebrates the beauty of imperfection.

Their recent Antao Earth washbasins showcase this approach. They have a dewdrop-shaped form and hand-glazed finish, with resulting variations in colour and texture giving a tactile appeal.

A further contribution from Haas comes in the form of two new product additions to Villeroy & Boch's colour-focused Artis collection: Artis Sense and Artis Frame.

Artis Sense is a surface-mounted washbasin with a delicate expression inspired by textiles, while Artis Frame is a complementary bathroom furniture design bringing the lightweight, modern look of open metal shelving.

Villeroy & Boch is one of Europe's oldest and most respected names in ceramics, with a history stretching back 278 years and involving the merger of two great German ceramics families.

Today, the company focuses on two divergent ceramics categories – bathroom products and tableware – but always with a focus on innovative design and manufacturing.

Take a short tour of the recently opened Obama Presidential Center in Chicago, USA, is this video filmed by Dezeen.

Designed by US studio Tod Williams Billie Tsien Architects to honour US president Barack Obama, the complex in the South Side of Chicago opened to the public in June.

This short video shows a visit to the presidential centre, which includes a 69-metre-tall (226-feet-tall), granite-clad tower, plaza and public library.

 

View this post on Instagram

 

A post shared by Dezeen (@dezeen)

This video shows inside the Obama Presidential Center

The monumental tower contains a multi-floor exhibition dedicated to the former president and is topped by the Skyroom, which has views across the city.

Alongside the tower are a series of low-lying buildings arranged around a central plaza. These contain a Chicago Public Library branch and a building with an auditorium and large restaurant.

These buildings were topped with landscaping and gardens that connect to the wider Jackson Park, which was designed in the late 19th century by American landscape architect Frederick Law Olmsted.

We recently rounded up all of the other presidential libraries across the USA, dedicated to presidents from Herbert Hoover to George W Bush.

The lead image is courtesy of the Obama Foundation.

item.content:encoded:
Dezeen School Shows: a lamp crafted from minimally processed wood is among designs by participants of New Designers that will be displayed during the London Design Festival this year.

Also included is a mirror framed with a distinctive ripple-like structure, and candle holders sculpted from coloured porcelain.

New Designers

Institution: New Designers

School statement:

"New Designers Selects (ND Selects) is heading to Shoreditch this September, bringing a new generation of emerging design talent to the heart of London Design Festival.

"For the first time outside New Designers' flagship July showcase, ND Selects at Shoreditch Design Week will present a curated selection of young design businesses, typically one to five years into their careers.

"Running from 15 to 17 September 2026 at Kachette, 347 Old Street, the showcase is a new collaboration between New Designers and Shoreditch Design Week.

"The event will take place in what will be London Design Festival's biggest district and offering emerging practices a platform to connect with the wider design industry."

Hem Stool by Dan Davies Design

"I am a recent furniture design graduate from Nottingham Trent University, specialising in material-led, process-driven design.

"My work explores sustainability, circular principles and honest manufacturing, with a focus on creating refined, functional pieces that are built to last.

"I currently work as a circular designer at Lamington Group, designing furniture and products using reclaimed and waste materials.

"My practice combines hands-on making with an understanding of production, aiming to create efficient, durable designs with a clear and considered aesthetic."

Designer: Dan Davies Design
Course: Furniture Design
Email: info[at]dandaviesdesign.com

Serene Table Lamp by Jasmine Prime

"Jasmine is a product and furniture designer from London. Her practice explores the intersection of traditional craft and contemporary design, with a focus on natural materials and traditional techniques.

"She works predominantly with minimally processed woods and other organic materials, allowing their inherent qualities to guide form, structure and function.

"Her work often involves adapting time-honoured techniques to new typologies, seeking to preserve craft knowledge while giving it a new relevance within today's material culture.

"Through this approach, Jasmine aims to create high-quality contemporary furniture and objects that celebrate craftsmanship, longevity, and the expressive potential of natural materials."

Designer: Jasmine Prime
Course: Product and Furniture Design

Crackdown by Studio Soldout x LightOn Lighting

"Studio Soldout is an Istanbul-based design studio founded by industrial designer Ibrahim Fatih Satılmış.

"The studio develops lighting, furniture and objects with a focus on contemporary minimalism, cultural depth and production-ready detailing.

"Its work explores the relationship between material, light, form and atmosphere. Rather than treating decoration as surface detail, Studio Soldout approaches each object as a functional piece with a clear spatial presence.

"Materials such as metal, glass, stone and ceramic are often used to create calm, tactile and refined objects for contemporary interiors.

"The studio's process combines concept development, 3D CAD modelling, visualisation, CMF development, prototyping and manufacturing alignment.

"This allows each project to move from an initial idea to a technically considered object that can be presented, produced or developed further with manufacturers.

"Recent works include Crackdown, an award-winning decorative lighting object, and Moonside, a side table and lighting concept exploring transformation, wireless charging and changing light direction through a moon-inspired form.

"Through these projects, Studio Soldout continues to build a design language that is minimal, culturally aware and suitable for international design contexts."

Design studio: Studio Soldout x LightOn Lighting
Course: Product Design
Email: info[at]studiosoldout.com

Dune Candle Holder by Riolab Ceramics

"Riolab Ceramics is a London-based design studio founded by Chilean industrial designer Paulina Moreno Rios.

"With a background in industrial design, the studio explores the intersection between digital technologies and traditional craft, creating contemporary ceramic pieces that are both sculptural and functional.

"Working primarily with coloured porcelain, Paulina develops objects that celebrate form, texture and colour.

"Her process balances technology and experimentation with artisanal craftsmanship, blending slip-casting and hand-finishing to create objects full of character and tactile presence.

"Her latest collection, Dune, is inspired by the desert landscapes of northern Chile, where she grew up. The surfaces of the pieces reflect the movement of sand shaped by wind and light, where tonal variations shift from warm oranges and browns in daylight to deeper purples at sunset.

"With this collection, she aims to invite touch and evoke a sense of movement. The shadows across the surface of the pieces enhance this effect, encouraging people to explore and connect with these tactile objects."

Design studio: Riolab Ceramics
Course: Ceramics
Email: riolabceramica[at]gmail.com

What Holds by Irenehuang.Design

"My practice focuses on material-led furniture mainly with wood and ceramic.

"Through functional objects, I explore domestic space, material relationships, and how everyday use shapes meaning, memory and lived experience."

Design studio: Irenehuang.Design
Course: Furniture Design
Email: huangzixun530[at]gmail.com

Pure Apricity Lamp by Rosie May Ceramics

"Driven by a passion for lighting, my practice explores how light influences the emotional quality of an interior setting.

"Influenced by principles of biophilic design, my work considers how natural references can be reintroduced into contemporary interiors through form, texture, and tactility.

"Rather than directly replicating natural forms, I translate their rhythms and irregularities through developed processes that allow subtle variations in form and surface.

"My practice is fundamentally process-led. Through making, I investigate how material, thickness, and surface alter the behaviour of light.

"Working primarily with porcelain, I am drawn to its delicate yet durable nature and the way its translucency diffuses light.

"Using slipcasting as a method of control and experimentation, I refine wall thickness and surface detail to achieve a soft, ambient glow. Each piece evolves through refinement, balancing precision with organic form.

"Positioned between craft and contemporary lighting design, my work explores how porcelain and light can be used deliberately to define the character of a space."

Designer: Rosie May Ceramics
Course: Product Design and Ceramics
Email: rosiemaymarks[at]gmail.com

Kruller Midi Mirror | Walnut by This is Oink

"We're Lulu and Dan, co-founders of This is Oink, a design studio making home and bespoke goods from our workshop on a Dorset farm.

"Dan is a product designer and skilled maker, while Lulu is a graphic designer; together we've developed our craft at notable studios and major institutions across London and Melbourne over the past decade.

"Our creative practice grows through a process of experimentation, combining traditional craft values with the possibilities of modern machinery.

"We launched with our Kruller Mirror collection, characterised by its distinctive ripple form across a variety of timbers and sizes. Alongside this, our Timbre collection explores material contrast through turned bowls and our Timbre Lamp, defined by a continuous wiggle joint.

"Our work is rooted in process, combining traditional craftsmanship with modern machining to create playful yet refined objects for the home."

Design studio: This is Oink
Course: Product Design
Email: info[at]thisisoink.com

Tranquility by Ceramakka

"Ceramakka explores how sculptural form can bring the restorative qualities of nature into contemporary interiors.

"Inspired by the Japanese practice of Shinrin-yoku (Forest Bathing), Louisa Akka creates biomorphic ceramic forms that echo the cycles of growth, entropy and regeneration found in the natural world.

"Working with clay as an elemental and responsive material, each piece is shaped to create a quiet dialogue between form, light, shadow and space.

"The unglazed surfaces reveal the natural beauty of the ceramic material, with some sculptures meticulously hand-sanded to a silky, tactile finish, while others use a signature iron-transfer technique to evoke organic textures and tonal qualities of the forest.

"Material integrity and sustainability are integral to the practice, with single firings, no glazes and recycling of armature components.

"Created for residential, hospitality and architectural environments, Ceramakka sits at the intersection of contemporary craft and biophilic design, inviting a slower, more sensory engagement with space."

Design studio: Ceramakka
Course: Ceramics
Email: louisa[at]moorgate-orient.co.uk

Frame Stool by Caden Hao

"The goal of my design project is to create artefacts that invite introspection, presence and perspective.

"Within the concept of introspection, I'm creating objects that spark the practice of examining one's own thoughts and emotions to gain deeper self-awareness and understanding.

"This project is an exploration of how design can gently shift our attention inward, encouraging presence and inviting reflective practice.

"This collection of wooden furniture explores tactility, inviting a more embodied and intuitive way of sensing. A shallow inner slope on the sitting surface remains visually subtle, revealing itself only through physical engagement.

"The contrast between its visual lightness and actual weight prompts a moment of pause when lifting the piece.

"By creating tension between what is seen and what is felt, the work draws attention to the present and shifts focus away from purely visual perception."

Student: Caden Hao
Course: Furniture Design
Email: cadenhao522[at]gmail.com

Conchiolin Console Table by Phil Berczuk Design

"My creative practice sits at the intersection of the natural and the constructed.

"It draws on organic forms, raw materials and elemental processes, as well as the geometry and texture of the built environment, transforming these influences into singular pieces of sculptural furniture.

"The Conchiolin Series is inspired by the protective layered architecture of giant clam and oyster shells, exploring ideas of growth and transformation.

"Constructed from micro-laminated smoked oak veneer, the pieces are hand sculpted into linear rhythmic forms, delicately balanced across multiple components."

Student: Phil Berczuk Design
Course: Product and Furniture Design
Email: phil[at]philberczuk.design

item.content:encoded:
Accoya wood cladding and expansive terraces feature at the Dune House, which was designed by American studio Ziger Snead Architects for a tight site with many restrictions.

Tucked into a dense area, the home is located on Fenwick Island – a long, slender strip of land found just off the coast of Delaware.

The home fits a "demanding program on a sensitive site with a tight zoning envelope", said Baltimore-based Ziger Snead Architects.

The project was designed for a family who had summered on Fenwick Island for decades and desired a vacation home rooted to place.

"When they acquired a rare corner lot overlooking the dunes, they sought a home that would accommodate their growing family while fostering deep connections with the surrounding landscape," the architecture studio said.

The team conceived a bar-shaped, three-storey building that adheres to a 35-foot (10.7-metre) height restriction.

Along the east elevation, wide terraces cantilever over the beach and look toward the Atlantic Ocean. At the very top, the roof extends outward to form a trellis-like eave.

Facades are clad in a accoya wood that is meant to age over time.

"Left unfinished, the accoya weathers in the salt air, allowing the house to age in the landscape and contain time and place in its materiality," the team said.

Read:

Slate House by Ziger Snead replaces fire-ravaged Maryland home

Some areas of the exterior are lined with wooden slats, which "create a light, airy facade that softens the silhouette and generates shifting patterns of light and shadow throughout the day".

The house is entered on the ground level, which could potentially flood, prompting the team to avoid placing main living spaces there.

Instead, a mudroom, garage and gym occupy the bottom level, along with elements for beach living — outdoor showers, foot-washing stations and storage space for paddleboards and beach umbrellas.

"By elevating living spaces above the floodplain and using breakaway construction at ground level, the design also provides flood resilience," the team said.

The middle floor holds a lounge and four bedrooms, each with ocean views and access to terraces. The top floor encompasses the communal zone and primary bedroom.

"At the upper level, the house opens entirely," the team said. "The living, dining and entertaining spaces occupy a vast, open area that extends onto a terrace cantilevering 17 feet over the dunes."

Throughout the interior, one finds a restrained selection of materials and colours.

"The palette is muted and reserved, focusing attention on the views and surroundings," the team said.

Several custom pieces have a strong connection to place. For instance, sinks and a coffee table are made of concrete with sand from the adjacent beach. The dining table is crafted from a fallen ash tree in Baltimore, where the family is based.

Other projects by Ziger Snead Architects include a family home in Maryland with stone shingles and charred wood on the exterior. It was built to replace a ranch-style home that was lost in a fire.

The photography is by Jennifer Hughes.

Dezeen Showroom: German furniture brand Schönbuch and designers Jehs + Laub have updated their Stripes storage system, adding new finishes, accent colours and friendly shapes.

A modular and fully customisable system, Stripes has been part of Schönbuch's catalogue for almost 20 years and can be used to make sideboards, wall units and other types of storage.

It is recognisable for its painted, handle-free door fronts, with grip recesses between the doors serving as a design feature and giving the pieces their linear, "striped" appearance.

For 2026, Schönbuch and Jehs + Laub have launched a number of updates to the design, including the choice to finish these grip recesses in one of the brand's new wood veneers or accent colours.

There is also now the choice of five oak veneer and three mineral stone options alongside existing painted panels for sideboard tops, and new rounded end units that Jehs + Laub say make the Stripes design "friendlier and smoother".

“Stripes works almost anywhere, whether as storage in entrance areas or bedrooms, or as a sideboard in offices," said Jehs + Laub.

item.content:encoded:
Pale brickwork and ceramic tiles were used to highlight the dappled light and green hues of the woodland surrounding this home in Utrecht, completed by Dutch studio Jeroen Spee Architecten.

Named Villa Bilt, the home is located in the village of Bilthoven on a site surrounded by tall Scots Pine trees.

Jeroen Spee Architecten said it designed the home to "embrace" these natural surroundings, with gently curving corners informed by the position of the tree trunks and canopies.

"The home is designed as an embrace of these trees as an integral part of the scenery," founder Jeroen Spee told Dezeen.

"The fluid contour line of the house plays with the positioning of the Scots pines and nods to the surrounding landscape," he added.

Villa Bilt centres around a double-height kitchen and dining area, which opens onto a patio and garden with a swimming pool.

On either side, the main bedroom and living area project outwards to hug this terrace, where they are bridged by a narrow section of roof that has been pulled away from the home.

Glossy ceramic tiles line these two southern wings and extend into the dining room interior, where they reflect dappled light and green shades from the surrounding tree canopies.

These tiles are complemented by pale brickwork that defines Villa Bilt's exterior, chosen to provide a contrast to the green and brown tones of the landscape.

"The positioning of the house's structural planes supports beautiful vistas of the natural surroundings and gives a functional rhythm to the spaces, both inside and out," Spee explained.

Read:

Woonpioniers models adjoining Dutch homes on "a game of Tetris"

"In the indoor-outdoor atrium, a ring of ceramic tiles brings the inside and outside together," he added.

"This creates a special sense of intimacy where people gather around the dining area, which also serves as the true heart of the home."

The brighter, south-facing dining space contrasts with the more enclosed northern side of the home, where an entrance area is organised around a dark timber staircase between a study and storage.

Illuminating this area is a central section of perforated brick wall, which is lined internally with full-height openable windows that allow for natural ventilation.

On the first floor, a balcony-like landing overlooks the dining area below and connects two wings of bedrooms and a central block of bathrooms to the north, which are illuminated by another section of perforated brickwork.

Spee founded his eponymous studio in 2025, having formerly been a founder of Studio Prototype, where he worked on projects including the self-build Edge House in Amsterdam.

Another woodland home recently completed in the Netherlands is Villa MB, which Tom Kneepkens designed to "integrate living and nature".

The photography is by Robertino Nikolic.

item.content:encoded:
British carmaker JLR has combined the off-roading capabilities of a Range Rover with the improved responsiveness and torque of an EV for the brand's first all-electric car.

Powered by two 260-kilowatt motors, the Range Rover Electric creates more torque than any Range Rover to date and 20 per cent more than other motors of the same size, JLR claimed.

A newly developed traction management system responds to manage slip in as little as 50 milliseconds on any surface. That's 100 times faster than its combustion-engine counterparts, according to the brand.

It can also climb slopes of up to 45 degrees and wade through up to 900 millimetres of water – high enough to fully submerge the battery and motors.

"The defining characteristic of Range Rover Electric is its ability to perform across every surface, with effortless comfort and refinement," said JLR vehicle engineering director Matt Becker.

"The responsiveness and precision of the new driveline control systems, enabled by electric propulsion, perfectly support this. We're very proud of the result."

Read:

Why does everyone seem to hate the new electric Ferrari?

With 550 brake horsepower, the SUV can accelerate from zero to 62 miles per hour in 4.5 seconds.

Hidden under the floor, a double‑stacked 118.5 kilowatt-hour battery gives the SUV a range of up to 372 miles.

Visually, the design deviates little from that of a traditional Range Rover, save the grille, wheels and underbody, which were aerodynamically optimised to extend its range.

The company has filed 300 patent applications for different parts of the vehicle, including its battery and motors, which will be made at JLR's Electric Propulsion Manufacturing Centre in Wolverhampton.

The car itself will be manufactured in Solihull, as part of a major investment in its Midlands sites.

Other heritage car companies that have recently unveiled their first electric cars include Rolls-Royce and Ferrari, which recruited Apple alumni Jony Ive and Marc Newson for the job.

item.content:encoded:
Architecture studio MAD has revealed updated designs for the Danshuis dance centre in Rotterdam, the Netherlands, which will feature a billowing glass extension to an art deco warehouse.

Situated in Rotterdam's docklands area, MAD announced plans to transform the existing Provimi warehouse in 2023. The latest visuals of the design show plans for a curving glass facade added to the end of the building, which was originally built in 1923.

Informed by the flowing fabric of a dancer's skirt, the rippling glazing will enclose the dance centre's foyer, which will contain a spiral staircase connecting the building's four storeys.

Elsewhere in Danshuis will be dance studios, a gym, exhibition space, cafe, performance spaces, a public hall, and outdoor terraces overlooking the river.

"A pleated glass facade ripples like a dancer's skirt floating in the wind, forming the new four-story foyer of Danshuis Rotterdam," said MAD founder Ma Yansong.

"Its transparent surface captures drifting clouds, shifting light, and the surrounding landscape, while people meet and move through the space," he continued.

"As the boundaries between inside and outside dissolve, people move not only through the building, but through the changing sky, light, and nature."

Read:

MAD crowns Fenix museum in Rotterdam with "living room for people"

According to MAD, Danshuis will be the largest centre dedicated to the production and development of dance in Europe, designed to provide facilities for all dance styles at both professional and amateur levels.

It is set to open in 2030 along the River Maas, near MAD's recently completed Fenix Museum of Migration (Fenix), which was also built in a converted warehouse. The construction of Danshuis and Fenix is funded by the foundation Droom en Daad.

"Movement goes beyond architecture, becoming part of the character of the district," said Yansong.

"The beauty of human movement and the moments of dance will resonate with Fenix, creating a continuous dialogue between the two."

Projects recently completed by MAD include a spiralling science museum in Haikou and a cluster of bulbous galleries topping a museum in Shenzhen.

The images are by MAD.

item.content:encoded:
Images have been released of the Old Oak Common station in west London, which is currently under construction as part of the high-speed rail network HS2.

The design, led by architecture studio WilkinsonEyre and engineering firm WSP, includes six platforms for the HS2 line running between London and central Birmingham, along with eight conventional platforms.

Latest images of the station reveal its expansive two-storey concrete structure, which contains the high-speed platforms within an 850-metre station box 20 metres below ground.

The Old Oak Common station forms part of the first phase of HS2, which will connect central London with the West Midlands.

Once complete, it will be one of the largest transport interchanges in the country and the largest subsurface station ever built in the UK.

Renders of the design by WilkinsonEyre showed the station's spacious interior crowned with a large vaulted roof, which will feature integrated solar panels and openings for daylight and ventilation.

Framing the central concourse are large concrete columns set to support the station's roof. A neighbouring public park is also yet to be completed on the site.

"The architecture draws inspiration from the site's industrial heritage and is characterised by a spectacular vaulted roof," the studio said when the design was revealed.

"The vaults are integrated with an array of roof lights, providing excellent levels of natural light across the platforms and the means for natural ventilation."

Read:

UK's longest railway bridge reaches completion for HS2

All 14 platforms have now been built within the station.

Passenger trains along the route are expected to open between 2036 and 2039.

The HS2 project has been highly controversial as a result of its associated environmental impacts, and ballooning costs and delays. Updated figures revealed in May estimate the cost to now range between £87 and £102 billion.

Last year, the 3.4-kilometre-long Colne Valley viaduct designed by Grimshaw for the HS2 reached completion, becoming the UK's longest railway bridge.

The photography is courtesy of HS2.

item.content:encoded:
Dezeen Showroom: three-dimensional, clay-coloured linear details emerge from the coloured glazes of the Terramater tiles, created by Italian manufacturer Marazzi as an ode to vintage ceramics.

The Terramater collection is made with special glazes that blend with the porcelain stoneware tiles' red body during firing, creating richly textured surfaces.

The tiles are available in a choice of seven colours, including deeply pigmented hues such as blue Laguna and earth-red Cotto, and two surface patterns: Ritmo or Losanga.

Ritmo features a pattern of irregular parallel lines giving a dynamic effect, while Losanga brings in a classic lozenge-shaped motif.

Marazzi says the tile design hearkens back to 1970s ceramics with its embrace of the reaction between glazes and natural oxides, and that the choice of small-to-medium-sized rectangular and square formats reinforces this connection.

Frost-proof and resistant to deep abrasion, the Terramater tile is part of Marazzi's Crogiolo series of artisan-inspired designs and is suitable for both walls and floors.

item.content:encoded:
Japanese toy company Bandai has reimagined its cult video game Tamagotchi as a miniature wearable so fans can always have their digital pet to hand.

Designed to mark the product's 30th anniversary, the playable ring is only 28 millimetres long – nearly half the size of the original Tamagotchi from 1996.

The company's smallest virtual pet to date is kitted out with a tiny 0.56-inch screen and an egg-shaped case rendered in one of three metallic colours – gold, silver or pearlescent pink – befitting its dual role as a piece of jewellery.

The gadget's display is rendered in full colour, but its design was simplified over two years of development to use only 64 components, compared to the 116 used in last year's Tamagotchi Paradise game.

The game's diminutive size has, however, come at the expense of an integrated USB port for charging. Instead, the ring is now charged via an accompanying case.

Instead of the pinprick-sized buttons in the front, the game is operated via two buttons on the side, allowing users to hatch, raise, feed and clean up after their digital pet.

Read:

Sweekar is world's "first emotionally intelligent" pocket-sized pet

Its clear plastic strap is available in ring sizes 10 and 14, with a spacer included to allow users to adjust the fit.

The ring, available exclusively in Japan, will bring back 30 Tamagotchi characters from the last 30 years, plus a secret bonus egg.

Virtual pets are among a slew of nostalgic 90s gadgets, like digital cameras and CDs, that have experienced a renaissance in recent years.

Elsewhere on Dezeen, we recently showed off a Tamagotchi-style reading companion designed to make books more fun for children and the world's "first emotionally intelligent" pocket-sized pet powered by AI.

item.content:encoded:
Interior designer Kelly Wearstler has teamed up with fashion brand H&M to design a clothing line, which launches this week together with her H&M Home furniture collection that was unveiled in Milan.

The fashion collection will comprise eight ready-to-wear pieces with silhouettes that H&M describes as "relaxed and refined – unmistakably Kelly".

The pieces include a coated cotton trench coat, sequin skirt, collarless cropped leather jacket and a slip dress printed with a pattern of vases.

The clothes are part of a wider collaboration between H&M and Wearstler, who has also created modular furniture, vases and lamps for the Swedish brand's interior retailer H&M Home.

Working with H&M was a way to reach a larger audience, Wearstler told Dezeen in an interview about the collaboration earlier this year.

"I love that I can reach that higher collectible audience, but also now having this partnership with H&M and doing something that's super accessible, I love that dichotomy," she said.

Read:

"Repetition is a big part of my design language" says Kelly Wearstler

The ready-to-wear fashion collection, which launches this week, will only be available online, while the furniture will be sold in select stores.

The furniture line includes a chair, Poma, that can be transformed into a loveseat by combining two chairs, a lounge chair called Soluna that can be used as a sofa by adding more modules, as well as an armchair and a sofa table.

To complement the furniture, Wearstler designed a number of smaller accessories, including three lamps, candlesticks, vases and a clothing rack.

To H&M, working with Wearstler presented an opportunity to bring her "vision" to a new audience.

"Kelly is a very powerful female designer," said H&M Home head of design and creative Evelina Kravaev-Söderberg. "She's always had a strong design aesthetic, and she possesses a unique, bold, and confident design language – I tend to say she's not whispering."

"We want to showcase that aesthetic to our customers, to bring that vision to new audiences, and every design is unique to us – these pieces have not been seen before," she continued.

Wearstler also recently created her first-ever piano together with bespoke piano brand Timbra.

The photography is by Gemma Warren.

item.content:encoded:
London studio Piercy & Company has taken over an apartment in the north of the city and given it a new interior featuring custom timber joinery and a mysterious curved corridor.

Apartment 21 was conceived by Piercy & Company as a space for hosting private events and exhibitions, or for accommodating guests.

The design brings complexity to what was previously a highly minimal, open-plan home. The new layout brings contrasts of dark and light, with spaces revealed gradually rather than all at once.

Key interventions include the curved wall, directing focus to an artwork rather than to the bedroom, which is now hidden behind a concealed door.

Elsewhere, a floor-to-ceiling joinery element separates the main living space from a new study. This incorporates both a wall and a door, united by a large circular window cutout.

Piercy & Company co-director Fiona Neil said she and the team found "a sense of play and a joy in subverting expectations", rather than sticking with the tried-and-tested open-plan approach.

"We focused on changes in volume and spatial character, in the use of solid and natural materials, and in the human-to-human spark of art and crafted objects," she told Dezeen.

The apartment is located in a neo-Georgian 1920s building that was once part of North London Polytechnic but was converted into residential in the late 1990s.

It was previously the home of a gallerist who would occasionally stage exhibitions inside. This was how Stuart Piercy, Piercy & Company's founding director, first discovered it.

When the owner decided to sell, Piercy was keen to build on this tradition by using the 103-square-metre space as a testing ground for the architecture studio's recently launched interior-design arm, led by Neil.

The idea was to create a space where people can share meals and conversation, guided by the principles of neuroaesthetics.

Read:

EBBA founder's all-timber London apartment celebrates "alive and imperfect" wood

"The psychological and physiological effects spaces have on us lie at the core of our interiors studio," Neil said.

"Here, we had the opportunity to witness the effects of experimenting with the compression and expansion of volumes, and the response to natural materials and plays on spatial perception; that all feeds back into the studio's work."

The importance of hosting is made clear as soon as you enter. One of the first things you see is a wall of integrated shelving made from British elm, filled with glasses, tableware and a selection of cookbooks.

The kitchen is located opposite, with a wall cutaway that opens the space up to the adjacent living and dining room.

Piercy & Company collaborated with British furniture maker Benchmark on all the custom woodwork, including a 14-seat dining table crafted from British ash.

Other elements in the living space include a doughnut-shaped mirror sculpture by Poland-based Zieta Studio, iconic mid-century chairs by Alvar Aalto, Poul Cadovius and Nanna Ditzel, and textile drapes that extend from ceiling to floor.

The circular window cutout frames a view through to the study, which features a curated library wall and a mezzanine loft.

The mood is notably different in the more private areas of the apartment, signalled by the dark tones of the connecting corridor.

The bathroom incorporates a curved shower, lined with dark grey tiles made from compressed basalt chips, which Neil said "feels like showering in a cave".

The bedroom is tucked away at the back and is currently set up to double as a drawing studio.

Current artworks on display include pieces by Flora Yukhnovich, Jess Allen, John Virtue, Antony Gormley, Peter Cook, Guan Lee and Fabine Verbier, but are likely to change over time.

The studio also plans to introduce new furniture designs over time.

"We intend to keep evolving the space and using it as a testing ground for both materials and objects," said Neil.

"We are currently developing a light fitting with Hand & Eye; we will use Apartment 21 as a testing space at prototype stage and then later showcase the fitting in the space on a more long-term basis," she added.

"Hosting temporary curations of art and objects is something we also hope to develop."

Other interior projects completed by Piercy & Company in London include an apartment in the former BBC Television Centre and a refurbishment of an office building in Mayfair.

Piercy sees these projects as equally important as the studio's architectural output.

"I've never believed scale changes the intensity of the question," he said. "A tower has to meet the ground the way a handle has to meet a hand – with the same sense of connection, the same care for how a hand rests, a body turns, a pause."

The photography is by Jasper Fry.

Dezeen Showroom: the warmth of Sicilian stone is the inspiration for Italian brand Marazzi's Mystone Pietra di Sicilia collection of tiles.

Mystone Pietra di Sicilia combines the high-performance characteristics of porcelain stoneware with Marazzi's technological finesse and an elegant and subtle stone-look aesthetic.

The tiles feature a warm, compact base and only the lightest touches of veining, creating a look that evokes warm limestone or very delicate marble.

The tiles are created with Marazzi's 3D Ink technology, which creates realistic textures by matching structure and pattern, with differentiation between each piece.

The Mystone Pietra di Sicilia range includes a mosaic tile with an irregular finger-like shape, evoking the beauty of Mediterranean handicraft.

The tiles are suitable for both residential and commercial uses, with variations available for both indoors and out.

item.content:encoded:
US celebrity Gwyneth Paltrow has collaborated with Texas-based studio Michael Hsu Office of Architecture on the first sit-down restaurant for wellness company Goop, giving visitors "a new way to experience the brand".

Goop Kitchen Del Mar opened on 31 August and is located at the One Paseo shopping complex in San Diego. It is the first location of a broader expansion for Goop subsidiary Goop Kitchen, which plans to open additional locations across the region and New York City.

The interior design is coastal, with a mix of walnut millwork, banquets with striped upholstery, and a slew of textured surfaces, including a tiled floor. A black-and-white colour palette was used throughout. According to the team, Paltrow worked closely with Michael Hsu Office of Architecture and "personally curated every detail" to make the space feel "elevated yet welcoming".

"Gwyneth has a real design vocabulary, so we could go deeper with her than we usually can – down to the nuance of how a piece of stone meets a piece of wood," said studio founder Michael Hsu. "Her attention to detail made the spaces sharper and more considered."

Visitors enter a "dramatically veined marble feature wall", where an ordering system rests on a large wooden desk. Banquet seating is lined up against large steel-framed windows and spreads out into the centre of the space.

Details include brushed-metal pendant lights and two thin rows of black-and-white checked tiles on the floor.

The details were meant to align with San Diego's beach oceanside culture.

"Designed to feel elevated yet welcoming, the interior is anchored by a dramatically veined marble feature wall and layered with warm, natural details," said the team.

"The space works for everything from a weekday lunch or sunset dinner, capturing the sun-soaked essence of San Diego."

Read:

Michael Hsu designs Shake Shack's New York headquarters in industrial space

On the outside patio, the restaurant is outfitted with mint green metal chairs, marble table-tops and the same striped upholstery. Scalloped pagoda umbrellas lined with a black edge also fill the outdoor space.

Visitors can order dishes such as an assortment of salads and bowls. Goop Kitchen will also explore expanding the menu to "take full advantage of having its first sit-down restaurant", according to the team.

"The 92-seat flagship gives guests a new way to experience the brand, marking its first dedicated dine-in location," said Goop.

Goop Kitchen was launched in 2021 primarily as a takeout and delivery service and an "upscale fast-casual concept".

According to the team, it plans to open locations in La Jolla, downtown San Diego and Manhattan next.

The Goop brand has been controversial since its launch. Paltrow herself has drawn scrutiny on social media recently for reportedly planning a dinner party for AI CEO Sam Altman.

The Michael Hsu office has worked on a number of restaurants, including a Houston seafood restaurant and an eatery in Austin housed in a building from the 1890s.

The studio has also worked with larger chains before, such as designing the Shake Shack headquarters in New York.

The photography is by Michael PH Clifford.

item.content:encoded:
Dutch architecture studio MVRDV has designed the Woma mixed-use building in Miami's Wynwood neighbourhood with a central plaza and a facade broken up into colour-blocked sections.

Developed by Uribe Schwarzkopf, a firm behind several recent high-profile Quito buildings, Woma will have 163 residences in Wynwood, a former industrial district now known for its murals and entertainment facilities.

MVRDV designed the facade system to visually break up the building by using multiple different colours and varying the width and pattern of the spandrels and mullions.

This, according to MVRDV founding partner Jacob van Rijs, is meant to bring the building down to human scale.

"Woma is neighbourhood-oriented not just visually but also functionally," van Rijs told Dezeen.

"It prioritises human scale and pedestrian connectivity, while integrating abundant greenery, neighbourhood retail, amenities, and a diverse residential mix – becoming a place where people can meet, interact, and feel part of the community of Wynwood Norte."

The red, blue, yellow and green elements also reference the presence of the fashion business in the area. On top of the colours, some of the facades have been depicted with panels of scalloped mettalic mesh.

MVRDV said that, overall, the facade is "textile-inspired".

Furthering a relationship to fashion, the structure will also serve as a headquarters for Miami-based fashion designer Rosita Hurtado, who owns the site.

The entrance to her portion of the structure will be marked with a facade of golden, scale-like elements, informed by Hurtado's fashion designs.

Formally, the structure will have various setbacks and cantilevers that reinforce MVDRV's description of the structure as a series of "stacked blocks".

Read:

MVRDV wins competition for "new world wonder" in the Netherlands

The cantilevers showcase the thick external structural elements that slope and cross, giving the building a jagged exterior in places.

A central plaza will be accessible by a wide staircase that abuts Hurtado's facade, allowing visitors to move through the block-wide structure. In the plaza and on street level, some of the building entrances will be arched.

Woma will have green roofs, some of which will serve as social areas, as well as a rooftop pool. It will also have a rooftop pickleball court.

Uribe Schwarzkopf CEO Joseph Schwarzkopf related the building to a "mosaic", hinting at its status as an expression of the community.

"Cities are not made of concrete and glass – they are made of relationships," he said.

"Like Wynwood itself, Woma is a mosaic: a patchwork of identities, creativity, and community. The facade expresses the neighborhood's deep connection to art, craft, and fashion to create a building that could only exist on this block."

MVDRV has taken a similar approach when dealing with the patchwork nature of American neighbourhoods.

For its first US project, in New York's Harlem, which takes its name from a Dutch city, the studio created the multi-colour Radio Tower and Hotel.

In China, it has pushed this even further in the design for a cultural complex in Shenzhen, which features not only different colours on the facade, but different material types.

In its home city of Rotterdam, the studio also recently made waves with its winning design for a "new world wonder", a collection of bulbous volumes covered in greenery.

The renderings are courtesy of Uribe Schwarzkopf.

item.content:encoded:
Dezeen School Shows: a performing arts space for students influenced by the physical and emotional arc of performance itself is among the latest projects by George Washington University.

Also featured is a communal housing project designed for families, and a hair salon that serves as a therapeutic environment for African American women.

George Washington University

Institution: George Washington University
School: Corcoran School of the Arts and Design
Course: Capstone Studio
Tutors: Douglas Crawford and Melina Misri

School Statement:

"The Interior Architecture BFA programme at George Washington University's Corcoran School of the Arts and Design in Washington, DC, prepares emerging designers to shape thoughtful, engaging and responsive environments.

"At the heart of Washington, DC's only CIDA-accredited programme is a rigorous studio sequence that develops conceptual thinking, technical knowledge, visual communication and an understanding of material, light and human experience.

"Situated within an interdisciplinary arts school and major research university, students draw on Washington as an extended classroom while engaging with practising designers, alumni and professional partners.

"The programme fosters experimentation, collaboration and a strong studio culture, equipping graduates to contribute to the profession with curiosity, confidence and purpose."

Hairitage by Brianna Cole

"Hairitage is a hair salon and game cafe located in Shaw, DC, designed to unite the community through gameplay, culture and connection.

"The salon provides African American women a therapeutic environment where they can relax, express themselves and build meaningful relationships.

"The concept explores translating Shaw's vibrant personality into an immersive interior experience of dynamic contrast, using intersection, resulting in ultimate connectivity among visitors and creating a third place.

"Reflecting the lively character of the neighbourhood, the contrasting forms draw on Black cultural influences, including the geometric patterns and organic curves reflective of nature found in African textiles."

Student: Brianna Cole
Course: Capstone Studio
Tutor: Melina Misri
Email: Briannacole2704[at]gmail.com

Kairo by Fiona Sekerke

"This project reimagines the omakase restaurant as an immersive overnight experience built around the life and practice of the chef.

"Pairing an intimate dining ritual with an on-site chef's residence, the design dissolves the boundary between making and hosting, treating hospitality as something continuous rather than episodic.

"Guests move through a sequenced series of spaces: a sake bar, omakase dining room, tea room and soak, each extending the experience beyond the meal itself.

"Drawn from the logic of origami, the architecture translates folded geometry and material continuity into a spatial language that guides movement and perception, framing dining as an act of trust and shared ritual."

Student: Fiona Sekerke
Course: Capstone Studio
Tutor: Douglas Crawford
Email: fionasekerke[at]gmail.com

The Silk Road: A Fine Dining Chinese Culinary Experience by Justin Liang

"Chinese cuisine has long been embedded in American culture, yet its history is often perceived as just quick take-out and overlooked entirely. This project set out to change that narrative.

"By combining upscale dining with culinary education, the design creates a space where guests can enjoy and learn the stories behind this rich culinary tradition.

"Inspired by the Silk Road, the concept of flowing expansion guided every design decision, where movement and space branch outward from a single origin, much like history itself.

"The result is a culinary hot kitchen, learning kitchen and upscale dining space that honours its origins."

Student: Justin Liang
Course: Capstone Studio
Tutor: Douglas Crawford
Email: Justinliang109[at]gmail.com

The Nest Collective by Madeleine Keiser

"A communal housing project designed for families, this space reimagines the idea of a 'village' as an integrated support system.

"Family dynamics are evolving, with traditional single-family households becoming difficult to manage and financially unattainable. This project responds by applying the communal housing model to family life.

"At the core of the design, a central stair links residents through a continuous thread of movement and interaction.

"Communal spaces extend from this core, intentionally positioned to encourage spontaneous encounters and integrate community into everyday routines.

"Breaking down physical and social barriers, this design cultivates a community centred on collective support and shared experience."

Student: Madeleine Keiser
Course: Capstone Studio
Tutor: Melina Misri
Email: madbyrd[at]gmail.com

Verenne by Madison Nikic

"Verenne is an urban winery in Georgetown, Washington, DC, shaped by the concept of human erosion, where time, use and ritual leave a visible imprint on space.

"It avoids direct references to traditional wineries, instead creating an atmosphere rooted in material authenticity and quiet transformation.

"The front lounge along M Street supports a more social energy, while the Cady's Alley entry leads to a quieter sequence of tasting spaces.

"Movement is less about circulation and more about choosing a tone of experience. Low, warm lighting and deeply textured surfaces place focus on presence, allowing the environment to be defined by the people within it."

Student: Madison Nikic
Course: Capstone Studio
Tutor: Douglas Crawford
Email: mgnikic[at]gmail.com

Aroma – a Bookstore Cafe by Natalie Sagnerova

"Aroma is a bookstore cafe located in the historic Georgetown neighbourhood of Washington, DC.

"Bookstores and cafes have evolved beyond retail environments into 'third places' that foster community, productivity and connection throughout the day.

"Aroma merges these experiences into a cohesive spatial storytelling.

"The design is inspired by the transformation of coffee – from whole beans to crushed to finely ground – each stage releasing a distinct intensity of aroma.

"This process becomes a metaphor for the building's atmosphere: the ground floor is rich and dense with sensory activity, while each ascending level gradually softens, creating a lighter, more diffuse experience of space, scent and interaction."

Student: Natalie Sagnerova
Course: Capstone Studio
Tutor: Melina Misri
Email: natalie.sagnerova[at]icloud.com

Hygge Kontor: A Danish Style Workplace by Sophie Fridland

"Hygge Kontor transforms a Washington, DC-based architecture firm into a Danish-inspired workplace rooted in arbejdsglæde (happiness at work) and hygge (cosy contentment).

"Zoned areas balance open collaboration with focused quiet zones, while a public-facing cafe, lounge areas, sauna and cold plunge foster genuine connection and real conversation.

"Nature-inspired greens, browns, pinks and blues, layered with warm textures, soft lighting, and slatted wood create acoustic comfort and visual warmth.

"In a post-Covid world shaped by hybrid and remote work, the value of in-person connection has never been greater, especially for industries like design."

Student: Sophie Fridland
Course: Capstone Studio
Tutor: Douglas Crawford
Email: sefridland[at]gmail.com

Community Flux by Thanh Dan Do

"A space for isolated communities to peruse and share their food and wares. The non-white communities in the surrounding area reside in their own enclaves.

"While the project does not argue to break communities apart, it seeks to be a space where people can come together to interact with others who differ from them.

"As the movement between people with different points of view comes together, so is the importance of the use of areas designated for transition to facilitate connection.

"The word 'flux' can be used to mean a transition, but can also be used to mean a bond."

Student: Thanh Dan Do
Course: Capstone Studio
Tutor: Melina Misri
Email: tddreq[at]gmail.com

The Federal City Museum by William McKay Smith

"The Federal City Museum is a project that explores the history and heritage of Washington, DC.

"By drawing on the district's ecological and architectural history, the museum finds a palette of materials key to DC's development, such as Potomac Bluestone, Concrete, Cockeysville Marble and Red Brick.

"Partnered with an interior garden space stretching vertically throughout the project, housing a pocket of the Potomac wetlands ecosystem.

"By simulating the material and environmental experience of DC, the project invites users to explore and traverse the city's immense history through its central stairway and its interconnected galleries and exhibits."

Student: William McKay Smith
Course: Capstone Studio
Tutor: Melina Misri
Email: wmsmith607[at]gmail.com

The George Washington University Centre for the Performing Arts by AJ Jones

"The GW Centre for the Performing Arts unites the university's dance and theatre programmes, long housed in separate, disconnected spaces across campus, under one roof in the heart of Foggy Bottom, Washington, DC.

"The centre gives students, faculty and audiences a shared home to create, collaborate and perform together, embedding GW's performing arts as a staple of the broader university and city community.

"The design is rooted in tension and release, mirroring the physical and emotional arc of performance itself.

"A lobby atrium, cafe, mainstage theatre, black box and production workshops make up the programme, each space choreographed to sustain that journey from restraint to freedom."

Student: AJ Jones
Course: Capstone Studio
Tutor: Douglas Crawford
Email: ajjones.design[at]outlook.com

item.content:encoded:
Yesterday, the United States' highest court said that the construction on the above-ground elements of the White House ballroom extension can continue.

The Supreme Court lifted the temporary ban that was put on construction by a lower court judge in April, responding to a lawsuit by preservationists including the non-profit organisation National Trust for Historic Preservation.

This overturn means that construction can continue on the proposed ballroom. Officially called the East Wing Modernization Project, the extension was designed to replace the former East Wing building, demolished last year.

"Beginning with the merits, the government is likely to prevail in showing that the Trust lacks standing to challenge the East Wing project," the Supreme Court said in its ruling.

Designed by local architecture studio Shalom Baranes Associates after its first architect, James McCrery, was removed from the project, the structure has already had significant foundation work done as well as visible above-ground construction.

Construction likely to continue

According to the New York Times, the ruling addressed the relevance of the lawsuits against the project and not the legality of the project itself, which some say needs approval from the US Congress.

However, it signals that the project is likely to move forward and may be completed before the legality of the project itself is even clarified by the courts.

In a dissenting statement, chief justice John Roberts said the White House is "an iconic American building whose symbolism and history are wrapped up in its architecture".

"All the more reason to ensure that those responsible follow the rules in deciding what to tear down and what to build up at the People's House."

Read:

Dropcity exhibition explores the "performative architecture" of the White House

The project features an extensive military complex underground underneath a massive structure with classical architecture. Architects have pointed out the structure's lack of coherence, both in style and size, with the rest of the White House.

The building work around the White House has included a helipad, placed where an MMA cage was built to celebrate the country's 250th birthday.

Despite the injunction earlier this year, it appears that a significant amount of above-ground construction has been carried out. According to ABC News, a crew has been working around the clock on the project, which the administration claims is 65 per cent complete.

"Golden Age" says Trump

Trump celebrated the decision on his Truth Social account, suggesting that the ballroom is on track to be completed by 2028.

"I am pleased to report that the United States Supreme Court has just ruled in favor of the Ballroom/Military Complex being built without any further contingency, doubt, or threat," he wrote.

"We are living in the Golden Age of America, and this Building will be one of the Greatest ever constructed in Washington, D.C. When completed in the Summer of 2028, the magnificent Ballroom and Military Complex will be something that the entire Country is very proud of."

Read:

How Donald Trump is using architecture to reshape Washington DC

The construction on the site extends far past the original footprint of the East Wing, which was first built in the early 1900s before undergoing a renovation in the 1940s, before being unceremoniously demolished last year.

This construction includes a subterranean entrance and security check under the adjacent Sherman Park. The administration has also considered adding a storey to the West Wing of the White House.

Dezeen Showroom: an ocean-like swirl of deep blue, white and gold veining characterises the Pangea Blue marble offered by Italian stone brand Antolini.

Part of Antolini's Exclusive Collection, Pangea Blue is distinguished by its intense cobalt blue patterning and the mesmerising interplay between its dense and ethereal, milky-white areas.

"Pangea Blue is a marble that evokes the primordial power of nature's elements," said Antolini. "Its dusty blue and mineral grey hues intertwine in soft, layered movements, bringing to mind images of ocean currents, shifting clouds or ancient geological formations shaped by time."

"Pangea Blue combines chromatic intensity with visual delicacy in a surface both elegant and inviting, capable of transmitting a sensation of tranquillity, depth and a connection to nature in its most primal form."

Antolini says Pangea Blue has the ability to evoke both stillness and wonder, and excels in applications such as bedroom walls and master bathrooms.

The Exclusive Collection is a curated selection from Antolini dedicated to the world's most extraordinary natural stones sourced from the finest quarries.

item.content:encoded:
Mint-green metal signals the transformation of this former industrial shed in the Czech Republic into Šmeral Art Factory, carried out by local architecture studio KOGAA.

The exhibition and events space occupies a small shed within the complex of the still-operating Šmeral machinery factories in Brno.

It is the first intervention carried out as part of a plan to diversify the area and better connect it to the city.

Local studio KOGAA focused on retaining the industrial quality of the warehouse and giving it "a new public life", painting its existing steel trusses a shade of pale green and using them to frame gallery spaces.

"As the first completed intervention within the wider Šmeral complex, the gallery acts as a catalyst for its gradual transformation," founding partner Alexandra Georgescu told Dezeen.

"More importantly, it demonstrates how even small, strategic interventions can unlock the potential of overlooked industrial buildings," she added. "We hope it encourages neighbouring owners and stakeholders to see existing structures as opportunities rather than obstacles."

The site's boundary is marked by the first legal graffiti wall in Brno, behind which is a generous yard space repurposed for events and temporary installations.

At its northern end, a canopy formed by extending the shed's roof covers a performance area framed in mint-green steelwork, alongside a metal entrance door in a matching shade.

This green tone was chosen as a nod to the green finishes that once defined many of the factory's buildings, and has also been used for a series of wall-mounted chimneys that ventilate the building.

Inside, the Šmeral Art Factory is a single, long space illuminated by a polycarbonate skylight at the apex of its roof.

Read:

Red scaffolding surrounds temporary pavilion in India

The original metal light fittings have been hung from its mint-green trusses and refitted with LEDs.

At its centre, a block containing toilets sits behind a long bar clad in white corrugated metal manufactured within the neighbouring Šmeral factory.

"The construction of the indoor bar was carried out by Šmeral's own turbine makers using materials and fabrication techniques from their everyday production," said Georgescu.

"It is a small intervention, but one that captures the project’s ethos: creating new value through local craftsmanship, existing resources and minimal intervention," she added.

A group of temporary white walls were created for the exhibition space at the building's southern end, where narrow steel bars beneath the trusses allow for the installation of hanging works.

Other recent projects that have transformed industrial buildings include Teshima Factory in Japan by Schemata Architects, which saw a disused factory building turned into a cafe and brewery with a turquoise-green colour palette.

The photography is by Alex Shoots Buildings.

Technology company Dyson has launched the CameraJet electric toothbrush, which includes a mouthwash jet that is directed by a camera to remove plaque between teeth.

Named the Dyson CameraJet, the electric toothbrush is Dyson's first dental hygiene product.

According to the brand it combines brushing, flossing and mouth-washing into one device.

Described as an "entirely new way to clean your teeth", along with an oscillating brush head, the device "uses a camera to floss while you brush".

Set near the brush head, a 100,000-pixel macro-lens camera tracks the teeth to find gaps, which are sprayed with mouthwash.

According to the brand, this replaces the need to floss and the device was created in response to reports that 9 out of 10 people don't floss regularly enough.

"Flossing is an awkward and time-consuming chore," said Dyson founder James Dyson.

"Few of us do it even though we know we should. Dyson engineers and scientists have spent well over a decade understanding oral care regimes and how nasties build up in the mouth. Our research has shown that people consistently miss the areas where plaque forms: the gaps between teeth."

In response to the low levels of flossing, Dyson created an alternative method of removing plaque that utilises the camera-directed mouthwash.

The system was trained using 470,000 dental images to recognise gaps between teeth. Using an artificial intelligence-powered algorithm, it takes 28 images per second to track the teeth and predict gaps.

Read:

Dyson aims to "disrupt" with launch of first headphones

"We wanted to solve three fundamental problems: how to see those gaps, remove plaque, how to improve cleaning performance while brushing," said Dyson.

"By combining a camera, machine learning, precision fluid dynamics, advanced brushing technologies, connectivity and WiFi, Dyson CameraJet introduces an entirely new way to keep your mouth healthy."

The mouthwash, which is dispensed in a conical spray, is contained in a transparent, 12.5 millilitre tank near the top of the toothbrush.

According to the brand, this holder utilises a pump to be kept under pressure, which gives it an "anti-gravity" capability that allows the toothbrush to continue to spray when held upside down.

The tank is refilled in three seconds from a dedicated docking station.

Along with the device, the brand developed its own toothpaste and mouthwash for use with the Dyson CameraJet.

Available in Ginger Mint and Spearmint, the toothpaste was designed to be non-foaming so that it doesn't block the camera.

Dyson, which is best known for its innovative vacuum cleaners, also previously released its first headphones.

item.content:encoded:
Greek architect Elia Zenghelis, one of the co-founders of international architecture firm OMA, has passed away at the age of 89.

Elia Zenghelis, who was also an influential architectural educator and director of Gigantes Zenghelis Architects, died on August 30 2026. Further details have not been made public.

The architect was best-known as a founder of OMA, which he established in 1975 with Rem Koolhaas, Madelon Vriesendorp and Zoe Zenghelis.

In a statement shared with Dezeen, Koolhaas said OMA would not exist "without his exuberant talent".

"Elia Zenghelis, my teacher, has died," wrote Koolhaas.

"Today it is hard to imagine the state of euphoria about architecture and about what architecture can do that made him a great example, inspiration and partner in crime," the statement continued.

"His falsetto singing in our small New York living room, bent over a drawing board, designing at 2AM, will remain proof that architecture can make you happy. The generosity he invested – his entire life – in other people's talent is monumental. Our connection at a crucial moment generated the insights and energy to launch our project."

Zenghelis established AA's rulebook

Elia Zenghelis was born in Athens in 1937. He began his career in architecture after graduating from the Architectural Association (AA) in London in 1961.

Shortly after, he began working at Douglas Stephen and Partners, where he worked until 1971 while simultaneously teaching at the AA.

The architect, who taught at the AA until 1987, is cited as one of the key people behind the AA's rulebook and procedural guidelines, and for encouraging more radical, avant-garde discourse at the school.

Read:

AA council has put the school "in serious jeopardy" by dismissing director and should resign, says Elia Zenghelis

Four years after leaving Douglas Stephen and Partners, Zenghelis set up OMA, where he led the London office and later its Athens branch.

Elia Zenghelis and his co-founder Koolhaas are known to have shared an interest in Manhattan, with many of the studio's early projects being speculative conceptual projects set in the boroughs.

Among OMA's projects strongly influenced by Elia Zenghelis are the design for the Dutch Parliament Extension in 1978, and the competition entry for the Parc de la Villette in Paris in 1982, which Bernard Tschumi ultimately won.

He also led the design of the Checkpoint Charlie Apartments in Berlin, which were completed in 1990.

Architectural education was his central focus

Elia Zenghelis left OMA in 1987 to establish Gigantes Zenghelis Architects with architect Eleni Gigantes, completing projects such as the Ashikita House of Youth in Japan in 1998.

However, over the course of his career, working in architectural education gradually became his central focus.

Read:

OMA co-founder Madelon Vriesendorp wins 2025 Soane Medal for architecture

Following his time at the AA, he succeeded James Stirling as Baukunst Professor at the Kunstakademie in Düsseldorf in 1989 – a post he held until 2002.

He also taught at Berlage Institute, Yale, EPFL and ETH Zurich, amongst other leading architecture schools.

In 2000, this led him to be awarded the Annie Spink Award for Excellence in Education by the Royal Institute of British Architects, and he was later appointed Professor Emeritus at the University of Thessaly in Greece in 2009.

item.content:encoded:
Sportswear brand Puma has launched a kit for English football team Manchester City that was designed by a fan using an AI generator.

The shirt was designed using Puma's AI Creator, which is described as a "custom generative AI tool that turns written prompts into kit designs within seconds".

It will be worn as the team's third kit this season, marking the first time a fan-generated AI kit has been used by a professional football team.

"For the first time in professional football, fans were given the power to design a kit using AI with the winning fan-created design set to be worn on pitch this season," said Manchester City.

The white kit, which was created using the AI tool by a fan called Elliot, has a simple design.

It features a central two-tone sash that is half sky blue and half navy blue. There are blue accents on the shirt's sides, while the words AI creator are written inside the collar.

It was chosen following a competition to design a shirt for the club using the AI tool. Powered by Google Cloud, the tool quickly generates kits based on text prompts.

Elliot's design was selected from a shortlist of 10 following a fan vote, with more than 180,000 submissions made to the competition overall.

Read:

Manchester City unveils rain-covered kit "as a tribute to the famous Mancunian weather"

"Puma AI Creator represents a genuinely new way of thinking about how football kits are made and who gets to shape them," said Puma vice president teamsport Dominique Gathier.

"The volume of entries we received speaks to the strength of the Manchester City fanbase, and the design that came through reflects that," he continued.

"This is a project that sits at the intersection of technology, football, and community and we are proud to have been able to bring it to life."

Although this shirt leaned heavily on AI, Puma does not expect the AI to replace human designers.

"While tools like this will become increasingly important in the future, I don't see them replacing the role of designers," UMA head of product line management teamsport apparel Alonso Sanchez told Dezeen.

"The most successful football kits are built on a deep understanding of a club's heritage, fan culture, and ambitions, which requires close collaboration between clubs and creative teams," he continued.

"AI can enhance the speed in the process, but the vision and final decisions will remain human-led."

According to Sanchez, the main benefit that AI added was allowing fans to contribute to the design.

"What makes this kit truly unique is the role fans played in shaping its creation through the AI Creator Tool," he said. "Rather than using AI to design the kit on behalf of Puma, we used the technology to empower fans to become active participants in the creative process.
"The tool gave supporters an accessible and engaging way to quickly visualise their ideas, experiment with different design concepts, and express what they wanted to see represented in a Manchester City kit," he continued.

Although the kit was generated with the help of AI, some commenters online drew comparisons between the shirt and a kit worn by Chelsea in the early 2000s.

Chelsea's 2003 away shirt also has a white background with a dual-toned blue shirt down its centre.

Last year Manchester City's third kit was covered in rain as a "tribute to the famous Mancunian weather".

Lake Como Design Festival, London Design Festival, Detroit Month of Design and Tallinn Design Festival are among the architecture and design events featured in Dezeen Events Guide this September.

Other events taking place during the month include Habitare, Frieze Seoul, Downtown Design Riyadh and Maison&Objet.

Detroit Month of Design
1 to 30 September, USA

Detroit Month of Design celebrates its 16th edition, hosting exhibitions, workshops, talks, open studios, tours and product launches.

The events span a range of disciplines, including graphic, fashion, industrial and product design, as well as architecture, technology, mobility and sustainability.

Frieze Seoul
2 to 5 September, South Korea

The 2026 edition of Frieze Seoul takes place at COEX, presented in partnership with art fair Kiaf Seoul.

The event's fifth iteration showcases work from over 125 global galleries across three categories: Focus, Material Practice and Spotlight.

Alongside the fair, the event features talks, an awards programme, film screenings and live performances.

Habitare
2 to 6 September, Finland

Habitare is an annual design fair that takes place during Helsinki Design Week, spotlighting furniture, lighting and accessories.

This year, the fair and talks series explores the theme Plot Twists, championing unexpected, unconventional and experimental design choices.

The fair takes place at Messukeskus Helsinki.

Maison&Objet September
10 to 14 September, France

Trade show Maison&Objet hosts its second event of the year during the 2026 iteration of Paris Design Week, located at the Paris Nord Villepinte Exhibition Centre.

The showcase presents products across six categories: Decor and Design, Fine Craft, Fragrance and Wellness, Fashion and Accessories, Gift and Play, Maison&Objet in the City, and Cook and Share.

Lake Como Design Festival
12 to 20 September, Italy

Border is the theme for the latest edition of Lake Como Design Festival, addressing how creative, geographical and social boundaries impact design.

The nine-day festival enters its eighth edition, with exhibitions, installations, talks and pop-up shops taking place at venues such as Villa del Grumello and Villa Saporiti.

London Design Festival
12 to 20 September, UK

2026 marks the 24th iteration of London's annual design festival, which launches a range of events across 11 participating districts.

The programme includes fairs, exhibitions, installations, parties, talks, workshops, tours and open showrooms and studios.

Dezeen has launched the 2026 edition of its guide to the festival, accompanied by an interactive map.

Downtown Design Riyadh
15 to 18 September, Saudi Arabia

Design fair Downtown Design hosts its second edition in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, usually located in Dubai during its design festival.

Organised by the Architecture and Design Commission of the Ministry of Culture, the four-day event features projects by regional and global designers.

Tallinn Design Festival
28 September to 4 October, Estonia

Almost 100 events are taking place in Tallinn during its 21st design festival, each addressing the theme Future of Product Design, which focuses on sustainable production and inclusive pieces.

Programme highlights include the Estonian Design Awards (BRUNO) exhibition and gala, the International Design Conference and the Design Street market.

item.content:encoded:
Social housing in Spain's Balearic Islands has won this year's Obel Award for demonstrating that public administration can be "a genuine engine for change".

Carried out by the Balearic Social Housing Institute (IBAVI), the Balearic social housing model involved addressing housing shortages with a more sustainable approach to procuring, designing and building public housing.

We investigated the housing programme as part of our Social Housing Revival series.

It is the eighth winner of the Obel Award, which celebrates architectural contributions to people and the planet.

This year's theme was Systems' Hack, which required entrants to consider how existing structures can be adapted when they are no longer fit for purpose.

"What makes the Balearic social housing model remarkable is how innovative architecture can be found not just in design and material choice but also in procurement, policy and process," said jury chair and MVRDV founding partner Nathalie de Vries.

"Public housing shortages are not unique to the Balearic Islands; the same structural pressure is playing out in cities and regions across the world," she continued.

"What this model offers is a framework wherein public institutions can adapt to their own context along with proof that public administration itself can become a genuine engine for change."

Between 2019 and 2023, the Balearic Islands in Spain transformed the administration of its social housing, spearheaded by economist Cris Ballester Parets and architect Carles Oliver Barceló, who both worked for IBAVI.

The housing overhaul involved developing a model for the commission, procurement, design, build and inhabiting of public housing that prioritised local materials, circular construction principles and climate-responsive design.

It sought to quickly increase public housing without sacrificing quality, amidst a housing shortage and a limited supply of public rental housing in the Balearic Islands.

Read:

Four projects by RA Architecture Prize winner Cris Ballester Parets

The Obel Award praised the Balearic social housing model as an example of how public institutions can drive environmental, social and economic change.

"It's significance lies not in a particular building, material or architectural language, but in the way it connects public policy, architectural experimentation, environmental responsibility, local productive capacity, and dignified housing delivery as parts of one system," read the jury citation.

"The jury sees the Balearic social housing model as a powerful example of how systems can be transformed from within. By using public administration itself as a space for experimentation, the model demonstrates how public procurement, investment and management can become tools for systemic change."

According to the Obel Award, Ballester Parets and Oliver Barceló will use part of the prize fund to work on spreading the international reach of their Balearic social housing model.

Oliver Barceló renounced his personal share of the prize fund, which will instead go towards emergency housing initiatives in the Balearic Islands, and IBAVI also renounced the award and the prize.

Alongside announcing the Balearic social housing model as this year's winner, the Obel Award said it will launch a second award cycle, granting a prize to another initiative designed to the Systems' Hack theme in spring 2027.

Previous winners of the award include non-profit organisation HouseEurope!, which won for its contribution to promoting a more sustainable construction industry across Europe, and a "visionary" coastal defence system in New York City by landscape studio Scape.
