item.content:encoded:
Japanese architect Kengo Kuma has been named the recipient of the Andrée Putman Lifetime Achievement Award for 2027 by the Créateurs Design Association & Awards.

Kuma, who is founder of his eponymous studio Kengo Kuma & Associates, was chosen for his demonstration of "how architecture can restore the relationship between people and the natural world".

The annual award was established by the Créateurs Design Association & Awards (CDA) to recognise careers that have had an enduring impact on the built environment, and is the award body's highest honour.

It was launched by the CDA to commemorate the legacy of French designer Andrée Putman.

Winners of the annual award are determined by members of the CDA rather than through submissions, with Kuma recognised for his role in connecting people with nature, according to CDA co-founder Yuri Xavier.

"For more than three decades, Kengo Kuma has asked how architecture can restore the relationship between people and the natural world, and he has answered on every continent," Xavier said.

"Our members chose to honour not a single building but the entirety of that pursuit, in the spirit of dialogue between tradition and modernity that Andrée Putman herself embodied."

Notable recent projects by the architect's studio include the Japan National Stadium in Tokyo and the V&A Dundee in Scotland.

Kuma said he is "honoured" to receive recognition of his life's work.

"In my design practice, I consider myself a long-distance runner," he said. "I believe the most important thing is to keep running over the long term with a single goal in mind: achieving harmony between humans and nature."

"More than anything, I am honoured that the Lifetime Achievement Award recognises the entirety of everything I do," he continued.

The award will be presented at the CDA ceremony at the Shangri-La Paris on 16th January 2027. Awards across fifteen categories are also set to be announced at the event.

Previous recipients of the annual Andrée Putman Lifetime Achievement Award include Norman Foster, Tadao Ando, and Christian de Portzamparc.

item.content:encoded:
As Burning Man kicks off its 40th-anniversary event in Nevada, we rounded up the work of 12 architecture studios featured at the festival over the years, including BIG and Arthur Mamou-Mani.

Larry Harvey and Jerry James put on the first Burning Man Festival in 1986 as a solstice ritual. At the time, it consisted of a small event located in Baker Beach, San Francisco, where the group burned the first Man, the festival's annual effigy.

Since then, the festival has relocated to a swath of desert in Nevada, where festival-goers erect and dismantle the sprawling campus, called Black Rock City, each year.

The festival does not have music or performance headliners; instead, it's up to the attendees, called Burners, and organising body The Burning Man Project to create events, installations and activities for the week-long festivities.

Since its founding 40 years ago, the event has grown to approximately 80,000 people, with some early organisers saying the event is "barely recognisable" today.

Architects such as Bjarke Ingels have designed for the festival, and like many, returned to participate at least a second time.

Read on for 12 installations created by architects at Burning Man.

Black Rock City plan, by Rod Garrett, 1997

Burning Man's "resident architect" Rod Garrett designed Black Rock City's radial plan beginning in 1997 after attending the festival for the first time two years prior.

The desert village fans out in concentric semi-circles with the Man effigy at its very centre and its arched roads, according to a passage by Garrett, are "the life-blood of our city, allowing unfettered access and egress for people, as well as to the logistics of supplies and maintenance".

Temple of Whollyness, by Gregg Fleishman, 2013

The Temple of Whollyness was designed by Los Angeles architect Gregg Fleishman, who describes himself as "going a bit underground" after he began his visits to Burning Man in 2007.

His temple resembled a pyramid and was made of interlocking wooden units that were constructed without the use of nails, glue or metal fasteners.

Find out more about the Temple of Wholiness ›

Catacomb of Veils, by Dan Sullivan, 2016

San Francisco architect Dan Sullivan and the Catacomb Crew constructed this pyramidal installation to evoke Black Rock Point, a mountain peak that surrounds Block Rock City.

"It is a ruin of a previous society – a remnant of our collective search for moments of quiet, introspection and reflection," reads a project description from the time.

Find out more about Catacomb of Veils ›

The Temple, by Steven Brummond and Marisha Farnsworth, 2017

Architects Steven Brummond and Marisha Farnsworth created this 2017 temple from 100 dead trees to draw attention to the nation's dying forests.

"There are dramatic changes occurring in our forests," said Farnsworth. "Pines, oaks, and many other trees are dying in unprecedented numbers from diseases and pests such as Sudden Oak Death and pine bark beetles."

Find out more about The Temple ›

Galaxia, by Arthur Mamou-Mani, 2018

French architect Arthur Mamou-Mani used 20 timber trusses spiral upwards to create a point, which took six months of prefabrication and 140 volunteers over 22 days to assemble.

He revisited his creation of the Galaxia temple in 2020, sharing drone shots of its construction for the first time two years after its 2018 construction.

Find out more about Galaxia ›

The Orb, by BIG, 2018

BIG founder Bjarke Ingels and colleague Jakob Lange designed this giant inflatable orb for the studio's first foray into Burning Man in 2018.

The mirrored ball was anchored by a 32-metre inclined steel mast and was designed, in part, to "help Burners navigate the desert and find their way".

Find out more about The Orb›

Steam of Life, by JKMM Architects, 2019

JKMM Architects worked with Finnish creative collaborative Sauna on Fire to create a traditional Finnish sauna experience for 2019 Burners.

The installation was made of timber slabs stacked on top of each other to form a sort of spiral, where an external walkway leads to a steam room, and then out to a central open-air atrium.

Find out more about Steam of Life ›

Solar Shrine, by Antwane Lee, 2022

Chicago architect Antwane Lee created the Solar Shrine as an ode to the waxing and waning power of the Sun as it moves from East to West.

The structure shot flames into the air and was made of lumber wrapped in plywood to create a smooth exterior.

Find out more about Solar Shrine ›

Project Carillon, by Steven Brummond, 2022

Steven Brummond used strips of recycled plywood for his 48-foot-tall (14-metre-tall) Project Carillon structure, which were arranged to resemble a fishbone or porcupine, according to the designer.

Festival-goers could also scramble up its sides to play with a set of ropes connected to 99 bells installed at the height of the structure.

Find out more about Project Carillon ›

The Reactor Project, by Assaf Allouche, 2023

Panamanian architect Assaf Allouche has produced several iterations of the Reactor Project over the years, a structure that is primarily made of wooden slats lined with LEDs.

"The structure is a meeting point and melting pot for the wanderers," said the team.

Find out more about The Reactor Project ›

Temple of Together, by Caroline Ghosn, 2024

California-based artist Caroline Ghosn worked with architect Maissa Sader of Kamai Studio to create the Temple of Together, an intricate structure that combines church architecture with Lebanese weaving techniques.

The interior features a series of chambers with a central, lit column that extends skywards.

Find out more about the Temple of Together ›

Temple of the Deep, by Miguel Arraiz, 2025

The 2025 Temple of the Deep was informed by natural sanctuaries, such as caves, and Baroque architecture, according to architect Miguel Arraiz. It was designed as a place of healing.

"Like a heart shattered into a thousand pieces, it bears visible scars – reminders of the pain that forged resilience," he said.

Find out more about the Temple of the Deep ›

item.content:encoded:
Portuguese studio António Costa Lima Arquitectos has completed Praia do Bom Sucesso, a block of three homes in Lisbon with an industrial-feeling structure of exposed brickwork and weathered steel.

Located close to the northern bank of the Tagus river, the new block was tucked behind the retained facade of an old warehouse, in an area that was dominated by industrial buildings in the early 20th century.

Informed by this history, António Costa Lima Arquitectos decided to evoke a warehouse, creating a brick and steel form that is concealed by the historic facade to the north but opens up to the south with balconies and full-height glazing framed.

"The building is gradually 'decomposed' by the subtraction of its volume, creating a difference between both sides of the building," founder António Costa Lima told Dezeen.

"A harder and opaque plane on the north side and a light transparent composition revealing the new metallic skeleton on the south," he continued.

"The preservation of the North facade that faces Rua da Praia do Bom Sucesso allows a chronological testimony that makes the morphological transition on both sides of the building."

Given the depth of the site, the studio divided the block into two long, gabled volumes that sit on either side of a row of three courtyards, which have been wrapped by glazing and perforated brickwork that pulls daylight into each home.

On the ground floor, the bases of these courtyards form private patios and entrance areas opposite a row of garages, leading into the lower level of each home. Two en-suite bedrooms occupy the more enclosed northern sides of the houses.

Read:

António Costa Lima inserts brick home into an old Lisbon warehouse

Weathered steel staircases lead up to the first floors, where corridors lined by perforated brick walls connect living, dining and kitchen areas that are divided across either side of a glazed light well.

"Two volumes merge and partially separate in the centre of the lot, from which three courtyards are born, each one serving one of the three houses," said Costa Lima.

"With the fragmentation the interior space, we were able to use complementary natural lighting."

To the north, spaces are more intimate and dark, illuminated by small openings in the historic facade. To the south, the dining and living areas are framed large areas of glazing, and open out onto terraces sheltered by metal louvres.

Both the home's brickwork and brown steel structure were left exposed internally, complemented by timber floors and white walls, which in certain areas stop short of the ceilings to permit light from clerestory windows.

Previous projects by António Costa Lima Arquitectos include the transformation of a warehouse on Lisbon's waterfront into a home, inserting perforated brick walls within the shell of an existing stone structure.

The photography is by João Guimarães.

item.content:encoded:
A scrap-metal-and-glass lamp and a bed made from a stack of pillows feature in this roundup of furniture and lighting spotted by design and interiors reporter Jane Englefield over the past month.

Perron Pillo Bed by Willo Perron for Knoll

This generously proportioned bed by Canadian designer Willo Perron gives the impression of a freestanding stack of pillows that you can't help but want to collapse onto.

The furniture is the latest in Perron's lineup of bloated pieces created for American brand Knoll, which have a simple but extremely effective appeal.

Perron Pillo Bed also marks the first bed produced by Knoll in several decades.

Ice Cube by 91-92

Copenhagen studio 91-92 is tearing up the rulebook of Danish design, opting for vivid hues and shapes not typically associated with pared-back Scandinavian furniture and products.

To celebrate the 2026 Chinese Year of the Horse, the studio added playful pony sculptures to the tops of its 3D-printed Ice Cube lamps, which nod to the freezing temperatures endured during Copenhagen winters.

91-92's overarching goal is to create "everyday objects that we want to live with" – a brief that Ice Cube passes with flying colours.

Konstrunda side table by Andu Masebo for IKEA

London designer Andu Masebo first put himself on the map with Tubular Chair, a striking piece of seating made from stainless steel tubes used to create car exhausts.

Now a household name, Masebo just designed a duo of curving side tables for IKEA's Konstrunda collection, created to offer collectible design at an affordable price point.

The tables are a smart graduation from Masebo's breakthrough chair and an obvious celebration of his fluid style. And on top of that, they don't break the bank.

Gel Lamp by Public Parts

Public Parts is the brainchild of London designer Billy Easter, who makes hand-cast silicone LED lamps with interchangeable colourful silicone gels.

Beautifully soft to the touch, the lamps' removable gels mean that the user can oscillate between various mood lightings.

"The lamp itself is also made entirely from silicone, giving it tactile and durable qualities that aren't immediately obvious from its geometric form," said Easter.

OG-NM301 by NM3, Quadro Design and Andrea Ferrari

Stainless steel experts NM3 looked to the aeronautical industry when designing this lightweight metallic stool in collaboration with Quadro Design and Andrea Ferrari.

The Milanese studio wanted to conceive a durable but minimalist stool for outdoor spaces and showers, and paid particular attention to the tube-bending techniques used to create bikes when fabricating the furniture's subtly spindly legs.

OG-NM301 is typical of NM3, which has become a staple of Milan's design scene since its founding in 2020.

Fused by Audra Grays and Maxim Lester

Emerging London designers Audra Grays and Maxim Lester joined forces to conceive this desk lamp using bricolage – the French term for creating an object using whatever materials are available.

Titled Fused, the project is the culmination of offcuts from Grays' glassmaking practice and scraps from Lester's metalwork, combined to create an elegantly utilitarian lamp.

The collaboration is a reassuring reminder of how emerging creatives can get their heads together to cut material costs, while still producing interesting and functional products.

Fused will be on display during next month's London Design Festival, as part of the Kiln Shift exhibition by Clink Street Ceramics.

item.content:encoded:
Barcelona-based H3O architects has renovated a 19th-century house in the city's Gracia neighbourhood, taking care to preserve heritage elements while introducing quirky details like hidden windows.

Casa Plató is a formerly rural house that was transformed into a grand residence by the ancestors of its current owner, who added a tower, galleries, mouldings and balustrades in the late 19th century.

The house was in need of restoration, but H3O was asked to retain the authenticity of its interiors and gardens, which have featured in numerous period film productions.

"Casa Plató synthesises a double condition: it is both stage and dwelling," the architects explained. "A house that keeps a story alive, but that also allows fiction. A house that embraces what has been and what could exist in other cinematic realities."

H3O's project focused on the ground floor and adjacent outdoor areas, with interventions including expanding the kitchen, adding a bathroom and introducing new openings to brighten the house's central areas.

The architects analysed films shot in the house to help determine a strategy for preserving its identity by carefully restoring heritage elements such as the mosaic floors, radiators, mouldings and colour palette.

"We greatly enjoyed thinking about the project as a dialogue or continuation with the pre-existing building, but from absolute respect and with playful and intelligent gestures," the studio added.

"We did not want to create an intervention based on contrast or rupture, but rather an improvement through understanding what already existed."

The existing kitchen was subtly updated by enlarging the space and introducing elements that complement the original wooden cabinetry and marble sink.

Dark tiles echo the tone of the previous floor, while a white geometric cooker hood, a wooden shelf and a wavy wooden table enhance the room's practicality.

A new terrace adjoining the kitchen strengthens the relationship between the interior and exterior spaces, with deep-blue tiles used on the steps evoking those found in the existing courtyard garden.

The original bathroom was entirely preserved, and the studio also added a new bathroom that features clean lines and a minimalist palette that references its predecessor's modernist style.

A circular shower enclosed by a matching curtain forms the centrepiece of the room, which features white mosaic tiles, a dark floor and stainless-steel washbasins with a marble countertop.

Rounded shapes used throughout the bathroom also evoke the forms found in modernist architecture, including a circular mirror, curved taps and orb-shaped wall lamps.

Read:

H3O creates "unpredictable" zigzagging interiors for lightning-struck home

"Modernism recovered these geometries that are marine, part of nature and more organic," explained the architects, who also added a porthole-like pivoting window in one of the bedrooms.

"We found it playful to introduce these forms in elements such as the pivoting circular window, which works like an eye that opens and closes, allowing visual connections between rooms."

The house's most distinctive heritage spaces were preserved largely as they were found, including the dining room with its decorative wallpaper, plaster mouldings, tiled floor and cast-iron radiators.

Elsewhere, existing fixtures and fittings were repurposed to maintain a connection with the past, such as the salvaged marble surfaces in the kitchen and existing doors that were carefully relocated.

Previously dingy circulation spaces at the centre of the floor plan are brightened by the addition of three strategically placed windows, one of which is concealed behind a painting.

The generously sized garden was preserved as one of the few remaining green spaces in an increasingly densified neighbourhood, providing a link back to the house's rural roots.

H3O was founded in 2017 by Adrià Orriols, Joan Gener and Miquel Ruiz. The studio approaches architecture through a critical and experimental lens, with each project engaging directly with its physical, social and cultural context.

Previous projects have included a converted barn with zigzagging interiors and a communal blue tile-clad barbecue.

The photography is by Simone Marcolin.

item.content:encoded:
Grassy rooftops and PE rattan facades characterise Split Mass Residence in Indonesia, which local firm K-Thengono Design Studio designed with multi-level social spaces for the family to gather.

Located on a corner plot in Tangerang, the home's tiered, sloping garden roofs connect indoor living spaces with the planted outdoor setting.

"The main design goal was to allow a seamless sequence of spaces that keeps the family connected to one another, while also staying closely aligned with the surrounding landscape," K-Thengono Design Studio founder Kelvin Thengono told Dezeen.

"I chose the split volumes to provide different paths between the indoor and outdoor spaces, while naturally bringing everyone through the home's shared spaces and directing the family to the open rooftop garden above."

The home's first floor contains bedrooms, bathrooms and an open-plan kitchen, living and dining room.

On one side of the open-plan space, a glass door opens onto a sloping, grassy rooftop with an outdoor staircase that leads to the swimming pool and barbeque area above.

Read:

Sou Fujimoto tops coastal holiday home in Japan with sloping green roof

On the other side of the open-plan living area, an indoor staircase doubles as seating for watching TV and socialising, with wide steps leading to a gym at the top.

An additional outdoor green-roofed staircase rises over the gym, culminating in a rooftop yoga space.

The ground floor level at Split Mass Residence has an L-shaped plan wrapped in bamboo-textured concrete facades, with rooms arranged around a garden patio.

An entrance foyer and staircase protrude from the concrete base, cloaked in woven PE rattan panels made from recycled polyethylene terephthalate (PET), which were designed to let natural light and ventilation into the overhanging upper levels.

"The pattern in the woven handmade panels was designed as a celebration of Indonesian vernacularity," said Thengono.

"We liked the contrast between the two materials: the concrete gives the house a robust presence, while the woven rattan softens it," he continued. "It also filters natural light and provides a greater sense of privacy."

Other houses in Indonesia that have featured on Dezeen include a circular home in Lombok with earth-toned walls and a house in Bali made from reclaimed native woods.

A stone house embedded into the Greek landscape and a sprawling American home with a retractable roof are among the most popular houses featured on Dezeen this month.

Sky View, USA, by Olson Kundig Architects

A retractable roof operated by a handwheel crowns Sky View house in Idaho, which was designed by US studio Olson Kundig Architects to have views of the surrounding mountains, and clouds and stars overhead.

Board-formed concrete encloses volumes on the lower floor, while above, glazed facades in the living spaces extend along the landscape.

Find out more about Sky View ›

Within the Earth, Greece, by Alexandre Pavlidis

Architect Alexandre Pavlidis embedded this house into the coastal hillside with a series of stepped, sunken stone walls that open onto expansive, panoramic patios.

Situated on the island of Sifnos in Greece, Pavlidis referenced the region's stepped terraces used to grow olives and grapes when designing the home.

Find out more about Alexandre Pavlidis ›

Casa Nido, Spain, by Iterare Arquitectos

Local studio Iterare Arquitectos nestled a white cube into the brick shell of an existing building in Valencia to form Casa Nido, or Nesting House, which was designed to be intentionally pared-back and stark.

Existing openings in the home were filled in with concrete or limestone louvres, while at the rear of the property, an enclosed patio brings natural light in.

Find out more about Casa Nido ›

Ushas, India, by Evolving Radical Aesthetics

An open-air temple carved into a retaining wall provides space for meditation at this farmhouse in Kerala, designed by Indian studio Evolving Radical Aesthetics.

Made from locally sourced black granite stone, the home was arranged into three staggered volumes to follow the contours of the hillside, with the living room cantilevering over the outdoor temple to shelter it.

Find out more about Ushas ›

Cabin Sande, Norway, by Helen & Hard

Situated on Norway's Atlantic coast, Cabin Sande is a timber cabin built atop a stone plinth made from rock sourced from the site.

Local studio Helen & Hard topped the home with a planted roof, which is supported by 18 branching columns made from whole spruce trees, including their root systems.

item.content:encoded:
Foster + Partners has developed a showroom concept for British motorcycle brand Norton Motorcycles, including sleek metal display stands that present the vehicles like sculptures on a plinth.

The retail experience was developed as part of Norton Motorcycles' ongoing rebranding project, which aims to emphasise the company's engineering heritage while promoting a modern, global outlook.

Norton Motorcycles worked with Foster + Partners, along with the design arm of the architecture firm – Foster + Partners Industrial Design, to develop a retail concept that would redefine how its motorcycles are presented and experienced by customers.

"Motorcycles at their best are emotional, sculptural objects of desire," said the company's chief creative advisor, Gerry McGovern, who steered the project in collaboration with Foster + Partners.

"In our experiential stores, they will be presented in environments that reflect their precision and modernity."

Read:

Rebranded Foster + Partners Industrial Design set to produce wearable gadgets

The vehicles are displayed on individual podiums with a futuristic aesthetic that aims to highlight their craftsmanship, engineering and sculptural qualities.

Each podium integrates practical features, such as overhead lighting to illuminate the aerodynamic forms, along with storage drawers and an open cabinet for displaying accessories and equipment.

"Norton's history is rooted in design, engineering and craftsmanship," said Foster. "Our design concept seeks to be a contemporary expression of the company's heritage and the timeless character of its motorcycles."

The retail concept was designed to work across a wide range of formats and scales, from compact showrooms to flagship destinations.

The modular system can adapt to its context by incorporating various supporting features such as digital and interactive displays, as well as areas for configuring bespoke machines.

Norton Motorcycles plans to eventually roll out the concept to over 200 stores globally, starting with flagship locations across key global markets.

"Working in collaboration with Foster + Partners, we are placing in-store design and architecture at the heart of our resurgence, elevating our retail experience in a way that is clean, modern and compellingly desirable," McGovern added.

"The ambition is not merely to sell motorcycles, but to stage them – elevating their purchase from transaction to experience."

Norton Motorcycles was founded in 1898 and is known for its participation in events such as the Isle of Man TT race, as well as for its historical models including the Manx, Atlas and Navigator.

The brand was acquired by India's TVS Motor Company in 2020, which has invested in a new manufacturing facility in England as well as a visual identity and retail strategy aimed at reestablishing Norton Motorcycles as a producer of some of the world's most desirable motorcycles.

Foster + Partners Industrial Design develops products and projects for global clients, ranging from furniture and lighting to building components and transportation.

Among the projects completed by the studio, which rebranded and launched a dedicated website in 2025, are a collection of stackable tableware and a simple wooden chair informed by the efficient shape of an oar.

Dezeen School Shows: an art neouveau-style cafe and shop located at a racecourse is among the projects from Hong Kong Design Institute.

Also featured is a jewellery collection that symbolises healing, and a concept store that spotlights traditional signboards.

Hong Kong Design Institute

Institute: Hong Kong Design Institute
Tutors: Kentaro Nagano, Henry Chan, Haotian Man, Damon Yau, Popo Leung, Cheung Sui Cheung, Queenie Yuen, Perry Leung, Ken Wong, Anna Lai, Viola Shum, Cassidy Dung and Nelson Leung

School statement:

"Hong Kong Design Institute (HKDI), as one of the member institutions under the VTC Group, is one of the most influential design institutions in Hong Kong.

"It provides high-quality education to cultivate knowledge and professionalism, nurturing design talents to support Hong Kong's creative industry development.

"With years of experience in design education, HKDI brings together the strengths of its design departments – Architecture, Interior and Product Design, Communication Design, Digital Media and Fashion and Image Design – to provide over 20 full-time design programmes, preparing students for work-readiness with socially conscious solutions to meet the demand of the 21st century workplace.

"HKDI strives to provide flexible and diversified pathways from Higher Diploma to one-year Bachelor degrees conferred by reputable universities in the UK, or degree programmes offered by local universities, as well as continuing education programmes leading to postgraduate qualifications.

"Through an established network with over 40 overseas design institutions, HKDI students are connected to the world through international exchange and project collaboration."

The Aqueous Breath by Dorothy Chan

"Located in Mai Po, Hong Kong, The Aqueous Breath re-imagines the bird hide as a 'moored boat', bridging the urban ego and the natural world.

"Shifting into the Gei Wai, it facilitates a vital separation from the city to allow for a mental restart through nature.

"This water-driven healing is grounded in neuro-architecture. The visual movement of water and its acoustics are scientifically proven to stimulate Alpha brain waves and activate the parasympathetic nervous system to lower stress.

"The design guides visitors to synchronise with the rhythms of wildlife, catalysing a shift in human behaviour and fostering a coexisting ecosystem. Rooted in a handcrafted process, utilising a bamboo structure to preserve traditional culture.

"Clad in site-harvested bark to create a calming effect, the architecture ensures that human recovery and ecological conservation coexist."

Student: Dorothy Chan
Course: Higher Diploma in Architectural Design
Tutors: Kentaro Nagano and Henry Chan
Email: dorothychanpl[at]gmail.com

Feed the Fish – A Modular, Interactive Pavilion for Plastic Waste Awareness by Janice Chau

"This is a transformative pavilion designed to turn plastic waste into a participatory architectural experience.

"By combining a curved structural system with cross-bracing elements, the pavilion creates adaptable, dynamic spaces that respond to different environments.

"Its core innovation lies in engaging the public directly. Visitors are invited to insert plastic bottles into the structure – an act called 'feeding the fish' – making the bottle not just a recycled object but an active, visible component of the pavilion's anatomy."

Student: Janice Chau
Course: Higher Diploma in Architectural Design
Tutors: Kentaro Nagano and Haotian Man
Email: janicechau132003[at]outlook.com

Zend Garden by Yoyo Cheuk

"This series of outdoor fitness equipment for seniors elegantly combines zen aesthetics with gentle exercises.

"Research shows many elderly lack regular physical activity despite needing it most for holistic wellbeing.

"Designed for mental tranquillity and mild movement, the collection creates serene outdoor parks inspired by a sand garden to promote healthy ageing.

"It features a Tai Chi gentle pusher made from seven stacked giant pebbles, a pebble-stacking-inspired device for leg lifts and stretches, and a Y-shaped multi-person social seating bench."

Student: Yoyo Cheuk
Course: Higher Diploma in Furniture and Product Design
Tutor: Damon Yau
Email: yoyocheuk06[at]gmail.com

Rebirth by Chantel Shum

"This jewellery series Rebirth narrates a journey from breakdown to bloom, consisting of five pieces: necklace, earrings, watch, brooch and ring.

"Using blue-purple gemstones, sandblasting and polishing techniques, it visualises the process of healing, breaking boundaries and growing into a new self, exploring the power of rebirth after hardship."

Student: Chantel Shum
Course: Higher Diploma in Jewellery Design and Technology
Tutors: Cheung Sui Cheung and Queenie Yuen
Email: 20040629q[at]gmail.com

Future Age by Jason Lam

"Future Age is a lifestyle exhibition that leverages immersive virtual reality and 3D reconstruction technologies to envision human existence over the next 50 years.

"By exploring societal evolution under the influence of artificial intelligence (AI), the exhibition aims to transform Gen Z's apprehensions into a constructive dialogue, showcasing how AI can enhance, rather than replace, our future way of life."

Student: Jason Lam
Course: Higher Diploma in Visual Communication Design
Tutor: Perry Leung
Email: jasondesign60[at]gmail.com

雜招廣益 Collective Grocery Co by Rame Seto

"Street signs are everywhere around our city, and many of them hold a rich cultural heritage.

"In a fast-paced city like Hong Kong, traditional signboards are slowly being replaced with little to no preservation of sign culture.

"Collective Grocery Co is a concept store aiming to raise awareness of sign culture.

"Each product represents a local industry and how it connects with Hong Kong, in hopes of educating local audiences to cherish the abundance of the city."

Student: Rame Seto
Course: Higher Diploma in Visual Communication Design
Tutor: Perry Leung
Email: ramemonet[at]gmail.com

Slow Ding Ding by Koi Wong

"Hong Kong is famous for its fast-paced lifestyle, where people often rush through daily life without noticing their surroundings.

"This project explores how the iconic tram – a symbol of slow movement – can remind people to pause, observe and rediscover the meaning of slow living in a busy city."

Student: Koi Wong
Course: Higher Diploma in Illustration
Tutor: Ken Wong

Two Gilded of Lilies by Eleana Ng

"This story is about two failed experimental female subjects who desperately crave freedom.

"Just as they are about to be taken back by soldiers, a seemingly kind woman, Marina, rescues them, allowing them to experience the taste of freedom. However, secretly this woman doesn't intend to save them.

"This is a group project done by the Animation and Visual Effect Students. Eleana contributed as the producer."

Student: Eleana Ng
Course: Higher Diploma in Animation and Visual Effects
Tutor: Viola Shum
Email: lamzuozhe[at]gmail.com

Minute by Minute by Ben Chan

"While other cities stop using batteries, Harbor City promotes the 'Battery Project'. Five years later, 80 per cent of citizens join.

"70-year-old Lan and her gifted 17-year-old grandson Tse Chun live together. Lan buys a one-year plan. Soon, Tse Chun collapses during drama practice.

"The doctor prescribes expensive battery medicine. To afford it, Lan tries to cancel the plan but is forced to halve the dosage instead.

"Tse Chun forgets lines and loses his competition. Suddenly, the TV announces a free Battery River. Shocked, Lan calls customer service, but the line remains busy.

"This is a group project done by film, television and photography Students. Ben contributed as the director, scriptwriter and art director."

Student: Ben Chan
Course: Higher Diploma in Film, Television and Photography
Tutor: Anna Lai
Email: chan65767360[at]gmail.com

From Rust To Dawn by Yvonne Hung

"The narrative structure of 'One Thousand and One Nights' constructs dawn as a temporal symbol of redemption.

"Through the literary metaphor of Scheherazade prolonging her life by storytelling, daybreak becomes a liminal threshold between life and death.

"This literary device, which transforms an astronomical phenomenon into a strategy for survival, provides a theoretical framework for exploring the relationship between light and hope.

"This study establishes a visual paradigm that connects cultural memory with future imagination through a dialogue between architectural geometry, calligraphic rhythm and industrial structure.

"Transforming the decay into a new beginning.

"This is a group project done by the fashion image design students. Yvonne contributed the styling part of the project."

Student: Yvonne Hung
Course: Higher Diploma in Fashion Image Design
Tutors: Cassidy Dung
Email: hyyvonneeee[at]gmail.com

The Silence Tear by Swally Lai

"The Silence Tear is a conceptual fashion collection that raises public awareness of the enduring legacy of child labour.

"It powerfully connects the historical injustices of the Victorian era (1837–1901) with modern exploitation in the luxury goods industry.

"Through avant-garde silhouettes, deconstruction, and compelling narrative elements, the garments expose the physical, psychological and social traumas of child labour, emphasising the loss of safety and human dignity.

"The core concept revolves around the inescapable cycle: vulnerable children robbed of choice, thrust into perilous factories, mines and streets.

"Design details include fractured fabrics mimicking shifted bones, severed cuffs and hems symbolising lost limbs, and binding layers representing entrapment.

"Aimed at luxury consumers, fashion enthusiasts, policymakers and the public, the collection seeks to evoke empathy, challenge apathy and inspire action."

Student: Swally Lai
Course: Higher Diploma in Fashion Design
Tutors: Nelson Leung
Email: swallylai0508[at]gmail.com

Café and Gift Shop at Sha Tin Racecourse "Round" Cafe by Akira Ng

"The art nouveau movement popularised art and demonstrated the value of equality for all.

"The movement – just like the Hong Kong Jockey Club – promoted horse racing to the common people, allowing this traditional aristocratic sport to be participated in by the general public.

"As an art movement, it advocates organic, natural, wavy and flowing curves, making the design more dynamic.

"It looks like plants sprouting from the soil and is full of vitality."

item.content:encoded:
This waterfront residence overlooking Michigan's Grand Traverse Bay has been reimagined to include a "mosh pit" lounge by California-based Lauri Design Studio.

Willow Point was originally built in 2005 in a contemporary style, which lacked the warmth that its new owners envisioned for their quiet lakeside life.

They called upon Lauri Design Studio founder Jenni Lauri to bring out the softer side of the architecture, using natural materials and handcrafted details.

"For this project, every decision – from reworking the architecture to layering natural materials – was guided by how the home would be lived in, creating spaces that feel calm, connected, and meant for gathering," said Lauri.

The floor plan was completely reimagined to strengthen the relationship between the interior and the surrounding landscape.

Staircases were relocated, sight lines were cleared and views were framed – all while improving the overall spatial flow.

The glass-wrapped lower floor's interconnected areas include the kitchen, dining room, living room and family room, intended to be used as a large gathering space.

A new picture window created through a concrete wall provides the kitchen with a view of the forest, while textured Ceppo stone was chosen for countertops and surfaces due to its resemblance to Lake Michigan's sandy shores.

In the living and dining area, a beaded Kelly Farley sculpture is suspended from the ceiling beside a reimagined fireplace, and surrounded by a mix of soft and metallic furniture.

"Layered textures and sculptural furnishings create an atmosphere that feels both refined and welcoming, encouraging long conversations and quiet evenings overlooking the water," said the studio.

Read:

Wheeler Kearns wraps Michigan lake house with two tones of wood

The original steel switchback staircase in the centre of the dwelling connects all three floors, and was refinished in a metallic plaster to add texture and depth.

The main entry staircase was relocated and reconstructed with solid travertine, ash treads and a curved plaster handrail.

Upstairs, a family "mosh pit" was formed in a newly created loft space, providing a cushioned area for relaxing together with views across the lake.

"Inspired by the nostalgia of a sunken living room, it has become the family's favorite gathering place, hosting everything from card games and movie nights to afternoon naps and grandchildren playing after long days on the lake," the studio said.

The primary suite was modelled after a private apartment, featuring its own lounge and kitchenette, as well as an integrated Travertino Rizzi stone bathroom vanity overlooking Grand Traverse Bay.

"More than any individual room, the home was designed around the family's evolving traditions, creating spaces where multiple generations can gather, reconnect, and build memories for years to come," Lauri Design Studio said.

Michigan's extensive shorelines along three of North America's Great Lakes offer countless potential for waterfront dwellings.

Other examples in the state include a wood-wrapped house comprising three separate structures by Wheeler Kearns Architects, a multi-level home for "people of all ages and mobilities" by DMAC Architecture & Interiors and a residence with two wings that intersect at irregular angles by Snow Kreilich.

The photography is by Gavin Cater.

item.content:encoded:
A tilted facade with large glazed openings was designed to bring an adjacent forest "directly into the interior" of this home in the Czech Republic by Prague-based Papundekl Architects.

Located in a South Bohemian village, the single-storey home is contained within a modular timber structure, which has been topped by a mono-pitch roof and clad with pre-weathered metal.

In response to the home's forested site, Papundekl Architects designed a tilted, north-facing facade that opens up to the forest at its rear, while a more-traditional facade overlooks the street.

"The core concept is to channel the immersive experience and serene atmosphere of the adjacent, north-facing forest directly into the home's interior," studio co-founder Jan Bárta told Dezeen. "By maximizing the glazing on the northern elevation, the facade effectively dissolves the boundary between the living spaces and the surrounding nature, making the forest a continuous backdrop to daily life."

According to the studio, the home's materiality was determined by a strict budget – encouraging the use of local, readily-available materials like timber and standardised glass.

This resulted in the dwelling's modular timber frame, which is arranged on a two-metre grid and lined on its northern edge with slanted columns.

"The material palette was driven by local context, availability, and cost efficiency," Bárta explained.

"Highly cost-effective elements such as the monopitch roof, asphalt roofing membrane, and standard thermal insulation blocks – offset the cost of the expansive glazed facade," he continued.

"Furthermore, this sloping facade avoids expensive custom solutions by utilising a standard commercial glazing system typically reserved for office buildings."

Read:

Mimosa Architects shapes Czech cabin from "rock, river and fire"

Inside, the home's spatial layout follows the structure's two-metre-wide modules, with the living spaces and bedrooms occupying two modules each to create four-metre-wide rooms.

Between them, the service zones, including the home's entryway, utility room, bathroom and storage spaces, have been limited to single, two-metre wide bays.

Each of the spaces are linked by a corridor that stretches along the open-plan kitchen and living spaces at the centre of the home to bedrooms at either end.

"The modular layout establishes a clear spatial rhythm and internal order, alternating between active living zones and functional service areas to dictate the choreography of movement within the house," Bárta said.

"Pragmatically, this strict repetition of partition walls, structural framing, and glass panels minimised material waste and significantly reduced overall construction costs."

Light-coloured walls complement the home's exposed wooden structure to create a simple material palette for the interior, which is backed by expansive views of the forest.

Elsewhere in the Czech Republic, Mimosa Architects drew on a surrounding forest for its design of a rural cabin built from burnt wood and black metal, and BekArch converted a disused bakery workshop to create a skylight-topped apartment in Prague.

The photography is by Alex Shoots Buildings.

Traditional farmhouses often have thick stone walls that block the view of the natural vistas that surround them. Below, we've gathered six examples of modern interventions that instead open up historic homes to make the most of their setting.

Among the projects featured are renovations of vernacular stone houses set among Italian vineyards, in Portugal's highest mountain range and the UK's first Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty.

Normandy farmhouse, France, by Studio Guma

French architecture firm Studio Guma cut large openings into the stone walls of this farmhouse in Normandy to funnel light into the living room (top image) and open up the kitchen to a paved patio through sweeping sliding glass doors.

Concrete sills, pale steel lintels and aluminium frames help to blend these interventions with the building's existing stonework and exposed timber structure.

Find out more about this Normandy farmhouse ›

Delfyd Farmhouse, Wales, by Rural Office

Two larch-clad extensions create "pockets of space" at either end of this 1800s farmhouse on the Gower Peninsula in Wales, the UK's first landscape to be designated an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty.

The new west wing, created by local studio Rural Office, gives the home a light-filled dining and sitting room with panoramic views of rolling hills on one side and the coast on the other.

Find out more about Delfyd Farmhouse ›

Casa NaMora, Portugal, by Filipe Pina and David Bilo

In a valley at the base of Serra da Estrela, Portugal's highest mountain range, architects Filipe Pina and David Bilo have supplemented a farmhouse with two gabled volumes that step down the sloping site.

Instead of local granite, the new additions are rendered in board-formed concrete, with one of the gable ends fully glazed to frame views of the landscape and provide access to the property's garden and a poolside patio.

Find out more about Casa NaMora ›

House of Blue Lias, England, by Forgeworks

A love of mid-century American architecture informed this low-slung extension to a 19th-century farmhouse in Somerset's Mendip Hills – a range of limestone hills south of Bath that's also designated as an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty.

A hearth clad in that same stone forms the central axis of the new volume, connecting the house to a nearby barn and to a swimming pool terrace via floor-to-ceiling sliding glass panels.

Find out more about House of Blue Lias ›

Whitberry, Scotland, by Pend

Scottish architecture studio Pend used pink-tinged concrete and painted metal to reference the reddish sandstone facade of this heritage-listed Georgian farmhouse in East Lothian when creating its rear extension.

Inside, a full-height glazed corner now houses a reading nook that looks out over the home's walled garden, while a skylight provides extra illumination from above.

Find out more about Whitberry ›

Casolare Biordo Vecchio, Italy, by Studio Bressan

A former portico was turned into a double-height, glazed dining room as part of the restoration and extension of this traditional stone farmhouse, set among the vineyards of Asolo in northern Italy.

Studio Bressan's design blends contemporary materials like glass and metal with more traditional stone and concrete. "The aim was to enhance the memory of the building without nostalgia, instead highlighting its truest signs and character," studio founder Emanuele Bressan told Dezeen.

Find out more about Casolare Biordo Vecchio ›

This week on Dezeen, designer Simon Weckert unveiled a colourful camouflage shirt that stops users being detected by AI video systems.

Named Digital Camouflage, the shirt was developed in response to a pilot project to use artificial intelligence (AI) video surveillance at Berlin's Kottbusser Tor, which starts this month.

According to Weckert, the anti-AI shirt uses a combination of bright colours and patterns to confuse the AI-powered system by subverting what the system recognises as a person.

Also this week, developer Riksbyggen and creative agency BBDO Nordics unveiled three tiny apartments based on what a 25-year-old can afford to buy in Sweden today.

The apartment sizes were based on income data from three Swedish cities, Stockholm, Gothenburg and Umeå, and range from 1.9 square metres for Stockholm to 4.5 square metres for Umeå.

"We wanted to show exactly how much home an average 25-year-old can afford today, and let people experience that reality," BBDO Nordics art director Anton Bolin told Dezeen.

In other architecture news, the administration of US president Donald Trump said it may have to demolish the Kennedy Centre in Washington DC, as a result of an ongoing battle over its renovation.

A civil action filed this week by a Justice Department attorney stated that the administration may seek to demolish the Edward Durell Stone-designed building, which it argues is in a "financial and structural death spiral", and replace it with an amphitheatre.

Meanwhile, in New York, construction has begun for a skycraper jail designed by architecture studio HOK in the city's Chinatown.

The Manhattan Detention Facility is one of the four new borough-based structures designed to replace the city's notorious Rikers Island jail complex. It will be located on the same site as the former Manhattan Detention Complex (The Tombs), which was demolished in 2024.

Among our most popular projects this week were a sunken home built from stone on the Greek island of Sifnos, a grass-topped office in the Netherlands wrapped in bark cladding and an open-air temple and granite farmhouse on a hillside in Kerala.

item.content:encoded:
For its first brick-and-mortar venue, production company A24 worked with New York design office Leroy Street Studio to overhaul the city's oldest Off-Broadway theatre to host live productions and screen movies.

A24 purchased the Cherry Lane Theatre in 2023 with plans to maintain its status as a live-theatre venue and maintain its name. Working with Leroy Street Studio (LSS) and restaurateur Zeb Stewart, the production house then renovated the building's main theatre and overhauled the interior.

The project also included adding Wild Cherry, a speakeasy-like restaurant run by the group behind the city's popular Frenchette bistro, with interior design by Stewart.

The theatre links two brick buildings along a tight curve on Commerce Street in New York City's West Village neighbourhood. The buildings date back to the 1830s, when they were used for manufacturing before becoming a theatre in 1924 – the taller of the two once operated as a grain silo.

For the A24 update, Leroy Street Studio focused on synthesising the layers of bygone renovations the building had gone through, while paying respects to its history, such as colour-matching and repainting the theatre's bright red doors by working with the original painter.

"When we arrived, it had a very early 2000s renovation in place," LSS senior interiors associate Leslie Bailey told Dezeen. "We wanted to strip that back, celebrate some of the original features, and be mindful about what we were putting over it."

"A lot of our work was about peeling back," added LSS senior associate Alex Witko.

One of the larger projects was renovating the original main stage into a dual-purpose theatre for live performances and film. This required the addition of a giant screening rig, outfitted with speakers, that descends from the stage's upper canopy.

Updates in the space included exposing the original brick walls and replacing the seating with lush mossy green banquettes. It also required the studio to consider the vastly different audio conditions needed for the entertainment styles.

To accommodate a film screening, for instance, curtains are pulled across the walls, while they remain open for plays. The conversion can happen within a day if needed, according to LSS, as the theatre switches between programming often.

Elsewhere throughout the building, the studio built a box office that flows from the street into a lobby concession stand clad with the same ocean blue tile.

The lobby area is small, with an exposed brick wall and restrooms to one side and the entrance to Wild Cherry towards the other, which is concealed behind a deep red curtain.

For the restaurant, the studio developed a low, scalloped ceiling and then worked with Stewart to create a space with "texture upon-texture" to match an eccentric menu.

According to LSS, the team shaped the ceiling to protect sound from carrying up to residential units above the space, as the room was also once a small theatre.

Read:

Lights glow through slatted teak facades of Hamptons home by Leroy Street Studio

"Historically, when the black box theatre was here, and they would have to put on a show, they would call all the residents above and tell them to be quiet," said Witko. "There was no separation."

"One of the things that we did that I think was very successful in the space was create a series of boxes within boxes. So above [the ceiling], there are actually two more ceilings that separate the restaurant from the residential floors."

The Cherry Lane Theatre and Wild Cherry opened last year, with the venue slowly rolling out performances and screenings such as the play Weer.

It is A24's first brick-and-mortar location and joins other companies such as Amazon investing in live-performance venues.

Leroy Street Studio previously designed a Hamptons home and also curated an exhibition at its Allen Street Gallery during this year's New York design week.

The photography is by Brian Ferry

item.content:encoded:
Dezeen School Shows: an art market with large glass walls overlooking pine trees in Hong Kong is among the student projects from My ArchiSchool.

Also featured are a multifunctional recreational centre designed to preserve its surrounding environment, and a Buddhist art gallery.

My ArchiSchool

Institution: My ArchiSchool
Courses: Animation Summer Programme and Architecture Summer Programme

School statement:

"My ArchiSchool and students started to experiment with sustainable design and wooden architecture, in order to reduce the carbon emissions from concrete.

"The studio provides an introduction to architectural education and digital design for those seeking knowledge and skills to aid their future career aspirations.

"The Hong Kong-based organisation offers in-person and online courses to help young people develop 3D modelling skills that can be applied to future careers in architecture and urban planning.

"Geared towards children and teenagers between the ages of six and 18, the various stages of tuition start at beginner level, and progress to cover a range of tools, interfaces and outputs.

"A variety of programme packages are offered to those wishing to develop a wide range of skills over several sessions.

"These include architecture history and theory, personal research projects and portfolio development, while the most comprehensive package concludes with an exhibition of student work after eight months of study."

Gleam by Albus Oscar Chung

"Chung's animation project, Gleam, addresses universal inner fears to encourage youth to embrace everyday life.

"Inspired by the roots of banyan trees, he designed an art market as his story's setting.

"'Young people will no longer feel fearful if they can find their cultural roots,' Chung shared.

"In his story, a boy survives a childhood near-drowning in a gloomy subterranean lake and awakens with a glowing macro-vision.

"Years later, guided by sketches of a luminous upper world, he and two friends dive into dark waters, navigating metallic shadows and ancient black-bronze figures.

"His enhanced vision leads them through submerged machinery to a translucent barrier, offering a tantalising glimpse of the sky world above."

Student: Albus Oscar Chung
Course: Animation Summer Program

A Promise Across the Sea by Tiana Lui

"Exploring how love can span across two cities, Lui used her art gallery project as the background for this animation, sharing her perspective on life.

"Growing up in Hong Kong, Luke and his golden retriever, Peanut, share an unbreakable bond filled with playful afternoons and quiet companionship.

"When life's responsibilities force Luke to move to Tokyo, the pair are separated by the sea, but Luke promises to return every month without fail.

"As years pass and both grow older, Luke faithfully keeps his promise, cherishing every sunset walk and shared treat until Peanut's final, peaceful moments in his arms."

Student: Tiana Lui
Course: Animation Summer Program

The Cat in Thunder by Marvin Wu

"Inspired by his love for Japanese anime, Wu created his animation to share a heartwarming story set in the city.

"While strolling through a sunlit park, a man accidentally drops his phone, only for a stray black cat to retrieve it for him.

"Just as an unexpected storm erupts with thunder, the frightened cat darts under a park bench for cover.

"Opening his umbrella, the man gently coaxes the shivering cat out to share his shelter, turning a sudden downpour into a peaceful moment of warmth and quiet companionship."

Student: Marvin Wu
Course: Animation Summer Program

The Gem by Ayden Zhang

"'The art in the city shines like gems,' Zhang shared. 'And Hong Kong is a good marketplace for both art and gemstones!'

"Zhang drew inspiration from gems to design this project. The lighting effects through the stained glass windows make the art market shine at night in the city.

"Instead of using big glass panes, the small and elongated window design intensifies the visual impact, making it truly unique."

Student: Ayden Zhang
Course: Architecture Summer Program

The Coral Reef Island by Claire Lee

"Inspired by the organic form of a coral reef, Lee has designed an art market to celebrate marine life in Hong Kong.

"She wants the space to be playful and refreshing to attract more young art lovers. Floating decks lead to the main entrance, while clusters of art shops are arranged in a spontaneous, organic layout.

"Granite and wooden materials are featured to create a safe environment with tactile textures. Glass canopies serve as semi-open spaces and act as rainwater harvesting devices, collecting water for a man-made waterfall."

Student: Claire Lee
Course: Architecture Summer Program

The Stackable by Teddy Cheng

"Borrowing the form of a traditional Hong Kong tram, Cheng explores various ways to transform recycled materials.

"He designed his art market by stacking three tram-shaped boxes into a mid-rise building.

"The upper deck serves as the restaurant and cafe area, while the middle and ground floors house the exhibition space and art shops, respectively.

"'I wanted to create a multi-storey art market so that the existing trees on the site can be preserved,' Cheng explained, highlighting his commitment to green design."

Student: Teddy Cheng
Course: Architecture Summer Program

Portals of the Minds and Spirits by David Ma

"Inspired by cave temples, Ma designed an art market that incorporates a Buddhist art gallery.

"He aimed to create a spiritual journey by offering visitors a portal into another world. He chose to use fair-faced concrete for the entire building.

"Many people love art because they want to live a meaningful, spiritual life. Buddhist art is the portal they are looking for."

Student: David Ma
Course: Architecture Summer Program

Companionship and Love by Anna Chu

item.content:encoded:
Brooklyn design studio Craighill has designed the Swingtop Lighter with a swinging mechanism and snuffer as part of the brand's brief to pay attention to overlooked everyday objects.

The Swingtop Lighter is made from die-cast stainless steel in Craighill's Brooklyn workshop.

It features a lever that is pressed down to activate the flint mechanism while simultaneously lifting a set-in-place snuffer. The flame stays lit on the wick until the snuffer is swung back onto the flame, extinguishing it.

It was designed so that users can refill the fuel well, wick and flint. Two colours, a matte black and silver, were created for the project, with the silver variation featuring a playful ceramic ball at the top of the lever mechanism.

Seeing contemporary lighters such as the standard Bic as difficult to use, the design team at Craighill looked to historical designs, where mechanisms were both more ergonomic and playful than the contemporary disposable plastic variety.

According to Craighill co-founder Zach Fried, this, as well as many other of Craighill's redesigned objects, are meant to last longer and to reach for the feeling of the well-made that many older products had. Though pricey, it was designed to last for years.

"In a moment of planned obsolescence that is very real, we take the path of pursuing material quality," he said.

"We want to bring things forward that feel timeless, but also make sense in this present moment from a visual culture standpoint, and then to execute them in a surprisingly satisfying way, where so many times the things that we interact with daily are disappointing."

 

View this post on Instagram

 

A post shared by Craighill (@craighillcompany)


Craighill created a large prototype to demonstrate its design

The company has become known for its explanatory videos. For the lighter, it posted videos on Instagram featuring a massive prototype, explaining each of the design features and the problems with contemporary lighters.

It allowed the brand to connect the audience to details, while marketing the products and introducing followers to the studio's more novel designs, such as a glasses holder.

"Taking these very commonplace objects that people are familiar with, and getting very zoomed into some specific interaction or some specific detail that we on the design team kind of obsessed over provides this inroad for people to connect to [design] because it's such a ubiquitous object," said co-founder Hunter Craighill.

"But it's not reimagining everyday objects, but it's a little bit more expansive than that."

Craighill added that while the brand focuses on function, it prioritises playfulness as well, and the videos have a sense of whimsy with the oversized prototypes and personal engagement with the designers.

"I feel like we are like very rigorous in a lot of the design work, and then oftentimes there will be some kind of like wink or twist," said Hunter Craighill.

In the video's comment section, people point out and engage with the designs, sometimes critiquing them or pointing out the datedness of the mechanisms.

Craighill and Fried said they welcomed the debate, noting that many people seemed to resonate with the attention to detail.

Read:

Pentagram works with child refugees to design Ambessa Play flashlight kit

"And sometimes the purists do come for us on the internet to say 'this already was a thing'," said Fried. "We know that. We're adding to it, hopefully, and are in conversation with an idea that we find really compelling."

Hunter Craighill agreed, adding that he knows when it's "time to exit the comment sections."

The lighter was launched with the Whitney Museum of Contemporary Art.

Other everyday objects rethought for the present include an exhibition during 3 Days of Design of future-looking cutlery and a capsule collection by Massproductions.

Dezeen Showroom: for high-performance exterior protection, Spanish tile brand Exagres offers Exa-tech, a ventilated facade system composed of extruded porcelain stoneware panels.

Exa-tech is designed to give architects the flexibility to create a unique look through their cladding while also delivering weather protection and thermal insulation to meet contemporary requirements.

The system provides reliable thermal insulation, reducing heat absorption during warmer months and helping retain indoor temperatures in winter.

The double-layer design with a ventilated cavity improves hygrothermal performance, lowering moisture penetration, while also adding acoustic insulation to shield from the noise of the street.

Suitable for both new-builds and retrofits, Exa-tech brings with it the high-performance properties of porcelain stoneware, which is highly resistant to UV radiation, thermal shock, staining and chemical agents and has low water absorption.

Exa-tech is available in a range of designs – including full-body monocolours and digitally printed wood, stone and marble effects – as well as a range of formats from 80 centimetres to 160 centimetres in width.

Exagres is part of Tile of Spain, an association of over 100 tile manufacturers.

item.content:encoded:
Architecture practice Nodecraft Studio has created a farmhouse on the outskirts of Bengaluru from a cluster of poured-earth walls and concrete volumes linked by verandahs.

Nodecraft Studio designed the 279-square-metre weekend retreat, named Aalok Farmhouse, to be a holiday home as well as a space for hosting the clients' business meetings.

"Designed as a retreat for family use and occasional business gatherings, the residence required a balance between privacy and collective interaction," said Nodecraft Studio.

"This led the design to move away from the conventional farmhouse model of enclosed rooms connected through internal corridors. Instead, circulation is externalised, transforming movement into a sequence of shaded pathways, courtyards and framed views," the studio explained.

Nodecraft Studio describes the independent volumes as "pavilions", arranged in a staggered configuration around existing trees on site to create a space where "architecture and nature remain in continuous exchange".

Entry to the house is through the centre of the U-shaped main block, hugging a linear swimming pool embedded in the sloping site.

The living, dining, kitchen and worship spaces are housed here in an open plan, overlooking the pool.

Each of the three bedrooms was planned as an independent volume around the main block, each featuring a private verandah that appears to float above the site due to its slope.

Read:

Prithvi Architects winds mud-walled Indian house around existing trees

The bedrooms are connected to the main block by outdoor decks sheltered by deep overhangs, low-ceilinged verandahs and courtyards opening into the surrounding landscaping.

"The transition from the lush landscape to the low and intimate covered space, and finally into the open courtyard, creates a deliberate sequence of compression and release, making the journey to the bedrooms an experience in itself," Nodecraft Studio founder R Hemanth told Dezeen.

Soil excavated from the site was mixed with lime, cement and aggregates and moulded into walls – a technique called poured earth. Punctured with large glass openings, these walls line the volumes.

Nodecraft Studio used an inverted beam system to top the volumes with an uninterrupted roof that cantilevers over the decks and courtyards.

The earthy material palette of the structural walls was extended across the farmhouse to preserve the relationship between the indoors and outdoors.

Leather-finished kota stone flooring was used across the interiors, transitioning into "river-bed-finished" granite in the semi-open spaces.

Wooden furniture with woven upholstery was dotted across the farmhouse, paired with jute rugs and locally-sourced decorative objects.

"Aalok Farmhouse redefines contemporary farmhouse living by replacing the idea of a singular enclosed residence with a sequence of pavilions shaped by landscape," concluded the studio.

Nodecraft Studio is a Bengaluru-based architecture practice founded by Hemanth in 2023.

Other Indian weekend homes recently featured on Dezeen include a farmhouse built into a steep Kerala hillside by Evolving Radical Aesthetics and a Tamil Nadu dwelling by Madras Spaces built using a locally sourced material palette.

The photography is by Naresh and Nayan with styling by Shivani Raina.

item.content:encoded:
British studio Foster + Partners, in collaboration with academic institutions, has secured funding to develop an automated fleet of robots and drones for on-site timber construction.

Named SWIFT-Build, which stands for Swarm-based Inverted Fabrication for Timber Buildings, the proposal won a €4 million, three-year research grant from the European Innovation Council's Pathfinder funding programme.

The project proposes using swarms of robotic assemblers and lifting units to build modular timber structures, aiming to improve the sustainability and efficiency of automated construction.

SWIFT-Build robots will build structures from the top down

Foster + Partners is the industry partner in the winning consortium, which also includes academic institutions the University of Bristol, the University of Southern Denmark, the Technical University of Munich, the University of Pisa, the Delft University of Technology, the University of Birmingham, and the Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich.

The studio described SWIFT-Build as an inverted robotic construction system that builds timber structures "from the top down".

"Combining state-of-the-art robotics and integrated AI tools, SWIFT-Build's inverted construction method can adapt to various scales and uses, with the potential for wide-reaching applications," said Foster + Partners senior partner Irene Gallou.

"The focus on timber modular construction highlights the project's sustainable agenda, with circularity and flexibility at its core."

Read:

"Mobile robotic factory" deployed to create modular housing for LA wildfire recovery

The process begins with robots assembling the uppermost level of a structure on the ground, and then lifting the structure to make space for the level below to be assembled, and so on.

Layer by layer, ground-based robots and machines construct the structure, while drones will fly above to monitor the building progress and alert to any issues that arise.

"The robots share information continuously, allowing them to adapt and operate safely without constant human intervention," said Foster + Partners.

The research project will result in a full-scale demonstration of autonomous robots constructing a timber pavilion, which will be designed for disassembly.

Other robot-related stories recently featured on Dezeen include a centaur-like robot designed to aid humans doing dangerous jobs and a behind-the-scenes look at the company building America's first mail-order servant robot.

The image is by Foster + Partners.

item.content:encoded:
Fashion brand Longchamp has introduced La Maison Unique, a clothing collection that draws on British designer Thomas Heatherwick's design for its boutique in Downtown Manhattan.

The new line, which is named after the store, was described by Longchamp as an "architectural collection" and comprises seven pieces – a wool winter coat, two skirts, a silk scarf, a headband, a top and a bag.

Each of the clothes and accessories features geometric stripes in different green nuances, drawing on Heatherwick Studio's recent update of the Longchamp New York boutique that the studio first designed in 2006.

The La Maison Unique clothing collection's print, which Longchamp calls a "swirling geometric pattern", was designed to evoke the swooping, sculptural steel staircase inside the store.

"Drawing upon the artist's bold and daring bright green staircase, spiral carpets and striking sculptural touches, Longchamp brings New York's interior into some of its FW collection," the brand said.

Heatherwick originally designed the Longchamp shop 20 years ago. For the store revamp last year, his eponymous studio recoloured the stairs in the brand's signature Energy Green colour, which was also used for the new clothing collection.

Read:

Heatherwick Studio gives New York Longchamp store Energy Green makeover

"It's the idea of not destroying another shop, but actually adjusting it and adapting it going forward," Heatherwick told Dezeen at the time.

"My hope is that we can be a species of adjusters and adapters, but you have to start with making something wholehearted enough so that somebody would care enough to say, 'Let's not knock it down. Let's adapt it and adjust it and repair it.'"

The studio also added a textured green "three-dimensional" carpet to fit the columns in the upper showroom space as part of the renovation.

On the clothes, the staircase's undulating shapes have been transformed into more of an art deco-like print. According to Longchamp, the collection was designed to bring "fashion, art and design into perfect harmony".

Heatherwick also recently created a new rooftop terrace with a pleated shelter for London's Olympia and designed glasses for Japanese brand Jins that draw on the movement of liquid.

item.content:encoded:
German architecture studio Opposite Office has created a one-square-metre treehouse to work from, fixed to a tree at the Bauhaus University campus in Weimar.

Opposite Office designed the compact tree-bound structure, named Baumhaus Office, in response to high office rental prices in Munich, Germany, where the studio was previously based.

"Baumhaus Office is both a real office and a somewhat exaggerated response to the real estate market," Opposite Office founder Benedikt Hartl told Dezeen.

"Instead of competing with Munich's rental prices, we moved the office out of the rental market altogether, and into the trees."

Measuring around one square metre, Baumhaus Office was designed to accommodate up to three architects.

A ladder leads up to its cubic shape, which contains shelving, a desk and fold-down panels that provide additional workspace.

Overhead, a domed skylight gives views of the treetop foliage.

"Munich has become one of the most expensive cities in Germany to rent office space," said Hartl. "For a small architecture practice, paying a substantial amount every month simply to have a few square metres of desk space can feel slightly absurd."

"So we asked a simple question: How much office do you actually need to run an architecture practice? The answer is about one square metre – a laptop, a cutting mat as a modelling workspace and a tree."

Read:

Riksbyggen creates Sweden's smallest apartments to "make the housing crisis tangible"

Baumhaus Office was made from standard spruce timber planks sourced from the hardware store, with plywood panels partially covered in aluminium.

Two ratchet straps secure the office to the tree, with a matting material added as padding to protect the tree from damage.

"The timber is deliberately ordinary – there is no exotic treehouse engineering hiding behind the project," said Hartl. "The aluminium cladding, on the other hand, makes it waterproof and gives the small structure a slightly UFO-like appearance."

"The entire office is held in place by two very large belts," he continued. "No concrete foundation, no screws into the tree, no complicated anchoring system, just a very convincing embrace."

"In the first days it was a bit scary, but after a crowd load test under the surveillance of our engineer, we felt safe."

Hartl gained permission from the president at Bauhaus University Weimar to use the tree as the home for Baumhaus Office for a limited time period. He said the office can be disassembled and reinstalled on another tree "relatively easily".

"If anyone has a spare tree, preferably with a good view and no rent, we would be very happy to hear from you," said Hartl.

In Sweden, developer Riksbyggen and creative agency BBDO Nordics also made a commentary on property prices with three tiny flats designed to the square metres of housing a young person can afford.

Other treehouse structures that have featured on Dezeen include a self-built, triangular home clad in polycarbonate panels and a portable treehouse that can be towed by a bicycle.

The photography is courtesy of Opposite Office.

item.content:encoded:
Storied Finnish glassworks Iittala has unveiled Unda, its debut collaboration with Sabine Marcelis – a range of lamps and vases that required the designer to develop a whole new production technique in collaboration with the company's glassblowers.

The three-piece Unda collection, named after the Latin word for wave, uses mouth-blown glass to recreate the undulating reflections of light on water.

"I'm fascinated by the way sunlight or moonlight hits rippling water," Marcelis said. "It's a mesmerising, ever-changing dance. I wanted to capture that in a more permanent way."

Marcelis is known for manipulating reflective and translucent surfaces to mesmerising effects, as seen in her Candy Cubes and the best-selling IKEA doughnut light.

Her collaboration with Iittala – the historic 145-year-old glass company behind the Aalto Vase – is a natural extension of these investigations.

"Her fascination with light, opacity and transparency feels uniquely relevant to Iittala and glass," Iittala creative director Janni Vepsäläinen told Dezeen. "These qualities are fundamental to the medium, yet can completely transform our perception of a simple object."

The idea for Unda was born from a conversation between her and Marcelis about the particular quality of Finnish light, the low angle of the sun, how it glints off the water and its colour changes over time.

To capture this quality, the designer worked with glassblowers at the company's workshop in Finland – the largest glass factory in the Nordics and the only one left in the country.

Together, they developed a new technique for pressing the ripple texture into the inside of the glassware using welded metal grids, so it appears to be part of the material rather than something applied to it from the outside.

"Pressing the pattern onto the inside of the object is something Iittala has never done before," Vepsäläinen said. "It proved challenging, but through several trials and workshops, we finally succeeded."

Read:

IKEA debuts colour-shifting version of Sabine Marcelis's viral "doughnut lamp" at CES

The result is a cylindrical table lamp with a subtle wave pattern that becomes more pronounced when illuminated, as well as a vase that's also available in a jumbo-size version that's nearly half a metre tall and was produced in a limited edition of 500.

All are available in one of three colourways – the soft pink of Dawn, light umber Dusk and smoky grey Shadow.

Vepsäläinen sees Unda as a continuation of Iittala's existing work in using glass to immortalise the slippery qualities of water.

"Exploring fluidity and water is part of Iittala’s DNA," she said. "The first designer to capture the essence of water ripples was Aino Aalto. Her rippled drinking glass series, introduced in 1932, is the oldest design still in production at Iittala."

Also on Dezeen, we recently published an exclusive look at Marcelis' Rotterdam loft apartment.

The photography is by Sofia Kulianu.
